I hope that the Government has not become so cynical and arrogant that it can disregard the thousands of voices that are calling upon it to change its direction with respect to closing CFB London.

Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I have the honour to table a petition, having been certified correct as to form and content by the Clerk of Petitions. The petition is signed by some 250 residents of the city of Winnipeg. The petitioners express concern over the proposed development of a major mining operation at Shoal Lake, the source of Winnipeg's drinking water.
The petitioners ask that all possible measures be taken to prevent environmental damage to the city's valuable water resource. Mr. Ronald J. Duhamel (St. Boniface) moves:
That this House call upon the Government to take steps to enhance the federal commitment to the support of post-secondary education, scientific and technological development, job training and re-training and the battle against illiteracy, all of which provide the essential foundation for building a strong and competitive future for Canada.
He said: Madam Speaker, I rise in the House today to address, I believe, one of the most critical questions to be presented in this Chamber of late. I am delighted to be able to do so with able colleagues from all sides of the House.

I believe that education is absolutely essential to the growth of our nation. It is particularly important for the development of insightful cultural policies, meaningful social policies and effective economic development policies. Most great nations of the world see education as the critical cornerstone of its cultural, social and economic development, and its main tool to remain competitive, a leader of nations.
There are a number of important Canadians who have made very significant statements about the importance of education. I should like to share a few of their comments with the House.
A. W. Johnson of the Department of the Secretary of State in 1985 said:
It is a mark of the maturity and the state of advancement of Canada that it has long been taken for granted that an educated society is a richer society-socially, economically and culturally. And it is a measure of the state of development of our nation that we have given expression to this belief, this ethos, by making almost universally available to all who want and can benefit from them diverse forms and programs of post-secondary education and training.
Donald Savage in The Toronto Star in 1986 said:
-if we are to progress economically as a nation, we will need more, not fewer, university graduates in science, engineering and business management. If we are to survive in a competitive and frequently hostile world, we will have to know the cultures, history, politics and languages of our friends, our competitors, and our enemies. If we are to make any mark in the history of the world, all this effort must be suffused with the ideals of our civilization, its history, its philosophy and its literature.
Just recently Mr. de Grandpre in his report made the following comments:
On an urgent basis, the first Ministers find the appropriate vehicle to review the education/training systems in Canada in order to increase the responsiveness to the requirements of rapidly changing international and domestic economies. Such a vehicle should involve participation by both business and labour, and might take the form of a federal-provincial royal commission on education/training.
I believe that education must lay the groundwork for a flexible and adaptable workforce and also provide Canadians with the tools we need to grow personally and professionally. It is important that our education systems facilitate the matching of labour force demands and supply, but we must not overlook the need to have an informed citizenry which can participate meaningfully in the Canadian political process.
Supply
It is education which will allow new immigrants to participate fully in Canadian life. It is education which will allow our aboriginal people the opportunity to overcome barriers to their full participation in Canada and give them the ability to attain self-government. It is education on which we will rely to produce tolerance of others in Canada and to respect equality rights of minorities, women and other disadvantaged groups. Attitudes formed in part by our education system will create the Canada of the next century, unified or divided, economically vigorous or regressive, tolerant or intolerant.
The Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre, as quoted by Jeffrey Simpson in The Globe and Mail on May 30 had this to say:
Colleges and universities are experiencing higher student-teacher ratios, deteriorating physical plant, and aging laboratory equipment.
Hyman Solomon in The Financial Post on June 12,1989 said the following:
Chronic shortages and mismatching in many skilled trades is getting worse, not better. And apprenticeship programs are fraught with high drop-out rates and have few women participants.
Many Hon. Members will recall John Polyani citing the lack of opportunity for Canadian scientists. More recently the head of the Science Council of Canada, Geraldine Kenney-Wallace, said:
Canada is very much behind; that this will eventually have a definite economic impact-while the rest of the world is getting its act together, Canadians are still arguing over whether they should commission a script.
That is what the chairman of the Science Council of Canada had to say. She went on:
I think the consequences, quite frankly, down the line are in the pocketbooks of Canadians. In other words, there is going to be a drastic drop in the standard of living. We are already living on credit now-It's a good idea that counts in the first place. A good idea is the hardest currency of all.
A colleague of mine in addressing the problem of literacy stated:
Because Canada has almost 5 million people who could profit by improving their literacy skills, much of their potential will never be realized unless all levels of government mount a massive campaign of assistance.
There have been valiant efforts in a number of places, but much more needs to be done for this important

June 13, 1989
Supply
group of Canadians. I want to remind Hon. Members of some of the promises made by the Government.

In 1984, the Conservatives were, and I quote:
Resolved to double the Budget for research and development in
Canada by raising it to 2.5 of GNP-
-and they felt that-
The federal Government should negotiate long term, five-year
funding agreements with councils that dispense research grants.
The Conservative Party stated: "We are resolved to maintain the federal Government's present financial commitment according to the formula established in the 1977 agreement- We believe that the financing of post-secondary education is a major priority for both levels of government".

Putting it gently, there has been a massive retreat by the federal Government from the post-secondary sector and those areas of education in which it has been involved. It changed the formula for the transfer of funds in 1985 by reducing the transfer by 2 per cent. There was another reduction in the most recent Budget of 1 per cent. If one looks at those two cuts that have occurred over a nine-year period, because the others will have been in place for a period of time, there is a reduction of transfers for health and education of almost $24 billion and approximately $8 billion of that was to go to post-secondary education.
What are the results of that kind of reduction? Clearly there are few choices of course. Some people will say, and I believe there is some merit in that particular statement, that we have not heard an outcry from individual institutions. When one looks at Canada with its over 250 post-secondary institutions, it is very difficult to find out exactly what is being cut where.
What are some of the other results? There has been a massive increase in tuition fees across the country with the exception of Quebec. If you doubt me, talk to the student associations in the various provinces, within colleges and universities. There has been a mounting student debt. That has been acknowledged by government as well. There has been a continued deterioration of plant and equipment.
I must emphasize that this is one of the major problems we are facing in post-secondary education today. There is simply not enough money available to ensure that the plants are kept up-to-date or enough money to ensure that the equipment we require in order to remain competitive is in fact in place.
Let us look at training and retraining. There was an initial cut of $700 million. Now there is an infusion of $800 million. When we look at the $800 million, it is quite impressive. However, we have to look at it within the total context. Once the $700 million is taken away, $800 million added, and adjust for inflation, there is not a significant increase. It has been further compounded by a siphoning off of some of those funds to the private sector where there is the purchase of places going on during the last few years. This has in fact removed some important funding from our colleges and universities. In fact, that is contributing as well to the deterioration of plant and equipment and has made fewer dollars available for those activities that colleges and universities would normally pursue.
What are the results of cuts in training and retraining? Many people are asking some very serious questions about the private sector initiatives. Are these private sector courses equal in quality to what is found in the community colleges and universities? Are the controls in place? Is someone examining the curricula being produced, and is it being evaluated?
While some good work has obviously been done, at the same time I suggest that it would merit significant attention and an in-depth review to see whether or not this siphoning off has been in the interest of all Canadians. Some of the other results of the cut-backs in training and retraining are waiting lists of up to two years and longer.
Older workers are being victimized. Recently I talked to an older worker, 58 years old, who needed retraining. He was told that he would have to wait two years, but he had hoped to be able to retire at age 60. There is not much hope. I have a particular soft spot for older workers who have contributed so much to this nation. A number of causes, including the Canada-U.S. Agreement, globalization, and what will happen in Europe in 1990-1992, are having an impact on Canadian workers in all parts of the country.
June 13, 1989

Quite apart from the massive impact of the recent Budget, people are being put out of work and need retraining. We must be exceptionally sensitive to that need, especially toward those who are older.
One particularly significant effect of all these reductions is what I call the real hidden tax. There is almost $24 billion less being transferred to the provinces for health and education. There is a reduction in training and retraining, as well as in other areas. Very often, the responsibility for these shortfalls are turned over to the provinces and, depending upon the wealth of the province, they can either absorb them totally, absorb part of them, or not absorb any of those cuts.
When the province cannot absorb such a cost, it is passed on to the client who in this particular case is the student. This is one of the reasons why tuition fees are rising dramatically in virtually all parts of Canada. The cost is passed on to the province, which is then passed on to the student. When the cost is passed on to the poorer provinces and territories which are not as well off, veiy often the poorer students must pay a greater share. That is most unfortunate.
Let us examine research and development and the Government's commitment toward this area. As I indicated previously, the Government made a commitment to increase the contribution to 2.5 per cent of GNP. However, it is barely 1.4 per cent, about half of what is being spent in the United States, Sweden, and Japan. There are fewer scientists than in most of those nations.
We are losing our competitive edge. That is not only my statement; it is the opinion of the head of the Economic Council of Canada who made that statement a short time ago. The level field that would be provided by additional education in our universities and community colleges with additional research and development is getting bumpy, perhaps even mountainous. How can we possibly compete on an even footing with the United States if we will be spending significantly less on those very programs that would make us equal or better?
What are some of the other opportunities that are lost because of this lack of funding for research and development? There are fewer opportunities for good jobs for our youth. I believe all Parties are interested in the creation of jobs, but let us add another dimension, that is, the creation of good long-term jobs which will challenge the people of our nation and challenge our
Supply
youth to go forward and produce more, to obtain jobs that will make them feel good about being Canadian by providing some insight and a contribution toward our cultural, social and economic development policies.
I suggest that this is one area where we can make some very substantial investment and reap some significant benefits for the people of Canada, particularly the young people in our colleges and universities.
Let us examine student assistance. The cost of living criteria have not been changed since 1984. The total amount of funds available have been frozen. Everyone acknowledges that the part-time assistance program is a disaster. There are two statistics about it, not one of which is better than the other. Less than 1 per cent of the people are using that program. There is a mounting debt load for students and rapidly increasing costs to students and parents. There is a climate of uncertainty because of the fear of accumulating debt and being unable to repay it.
There is a great opportunity for Canada to produce new highly qualified people who could become the professors of the next decade. We will need many new professors because it is a group in our society that is ageing. There is no large pool to replace them anywhere in the world. What better investment than to ensure that our young people are trained so they can assume those responsibilities in our universities?
Almost five million Canadians require assistance in literacy. While there has been a commitment of $110 million over five years, that represents about $4.50 per student per year. There will be little change, if any. The potential of almost five million Canadians, which is the size of a number of countries in this world, will probably not be realized.
Let us look at some of the other reductions. We do not know what the impact will be on education of our aboriginal people, on women's programs, on multicultur-alism or on official languages.

Madam Speaker, I just quoted a number of reliable authorities that have pointed to a major retreat by the federal Government from the education sector. Transfer payments for education alone are expected to be cut by about $8 billion. Training and skills upgrading: there were cutbacks totalling $700 million, and they added

June 13, 1989
Supply
$800 million. However, if we adjust this amount in terms of inflation, there has been a considerable reduction.
Furthermore, some of these funds have been switched around and transferred elsewhere in the private sector.
As for research and development, we provide only half the funding provided by the United States, Japan and Sweden. We have fewer researchers than many of these countries, although this would be a magnificent opportunity to enable young Canadians to explore new directions!
Financial assistance to students: the total amount is frozen. There have been no cost-of-living adjustments since 1984. As far as programs for part-time students are concerned, they are a total failure and all sectors admit as much.
Regarding literacy training, the Government has committed $110 million over five years. This is about $4.50 per student per year. And when we look at those $110 million, we must realize that we are talking about 5 million people. I realize the federal Government is doing this together with the provincial governments but, as I said earlier, we must invest a lot more in this area.
There have been other cutbacks affecting multicultur-alism, programs for Native people, women and official languages. What kind of impact will these cutbacks have on education programs?
I did not mention the fact that the program of instruction for new Canadians, with the books they were given to get acquainted with Canada, has been dropped.
Madam Speaker, I want to ask the federal Government to rethink its priorities in education, not only for the sake of our youth and other Canadians who want to study and get a better education, but for the wellbeing of this country. If we want to enhance our quality of life and that of other countries, if we want to improve our economy and our competitive position, education must be the cornerstone of a comprehensive policy affecting our cultural, social and economic sectors.

speechtext:
Questions and comments, Madam Speaker! First of all, let me congratulate the Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duhamel) for his speech. I think that he raised some very important points and I can assure you that as Minister of State for Youth, a Member of this House and a member of the Government, I too am very concerned about post-secondary education and everything to do with training, including employment programs.
I can tell Members of this House in complete sincerity, Madam Speaker, that the Government is particularly concerned about the very high drop-out rate of secondary school students in Canada now. The Hon. Member for St. Boniface did not refer to it, but Canada has a drop-out rate of around 30 per cent. That is a five-year average, but you must understand that it is not easy to have a very precise figure. I think there is agreement in Canada that the rate is about 30 per cent. That is a very high rate, higher than in most of the industrialized countries with which we compete. And that phenomenon disturbs us. It is a disturbing phenomenon, especially for a country that talks about free trade, a country that- And I am from Quebec, you know, Madam Speaker, and in Quebec there is a lot of talk about entrepreneurship, people talk about it and have clear ambitions, except that at some point we will have to think seriously about our country's ability to develop skilled labour to be able to meet these new challenges and manage the new technologies. It seems to me that this in any case is a very important challenge for our country, Madam Speaker, probably much more important than most people now suspect.
There is work to do. I can tell you that I intend to talk about it a lot because there is also an important social problem. You know, we tend to look at employment and training from an economic point of view, but the social significance of employment is not sufficiently recognized in our society. And in our society, working is how we participate in it. We forget, but that is the social contract
June 13, 1989

here in Canada. Implicitly, you participate fully and totally in Canadian society when you work. The definition of employment itself is changing as well, but it is still based on work.
This means that our systems will have to be harmonized more, in any case, to be able to play this role and reach this objective.
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the Opposition Members for their great patience. We feel that they are eager to hear me. They want to listen with interest to what I have to say this morning, but I was rather intrigued by my colleague's remarks for the following reason. He said a lot about the problems that they feel, that they seem to see and have identified, but I am always a little puzzled when Opposition Members speak to us in the House, because it is extremely rare for them to tell us what they would do instead. You see, that is the problem!
I enjoy being a member of the Government and proposing things, you know, but I would like to know, when a government has to make choices, what they on the other side-the Liberals and New Democrats- would do instead! You will note that in his speech, he did not talk at all about what the federal Liberals would do instead. My God, what a puzzle! He gets elected to the House of Commons, pretends to be able to govern the country, comes to the beginning of a mandate, criticizes the Government, makes a long speech and is completely unable to tell us what they would do instead! I want to know, Madam Speaker, because the federal Government-our Government-has increased the budget for post-secondary education and health care, under one agreement, from $15 billion in the 1984-85 fiscal year to more than $20 billion for the 1990-91 fiscal year.
Madam Speaker, I have a feeling that the Liberals want to take the floor away from me!

If it is a question or comment. I would ask for your intervention and direction because, according to the

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
First of all, Madam Speaker, with all due respect, and I realize that there is a lot going on in the House at once, I can assure you that when I rose in the House, there were no other Members on their feet. So with all due respect, I did not have the impression I was jumping the queue, and I can only regret, and fortunately there are witnesses in the House today to see this-

I can only regret that the Liberal Opposition would try to cut off Members on this side from saying anything, because it does not want to hear what we have to say. That is what the point of order is about.
Since the Hon. Member for St. Boniface in his opening speech on an opposition day brought forward by them on such critical issues as post-secondary education, illiteracy, training, and re-training, and in the name of the Liberal Party of Canada, had absolutely nothing, zero per cent, to say about what they would do if they were the Government, could he please give us an indication,

June 13, 1989
Supply
just a little idea of what little thoughts they may have on these issues?

Madam Speaker, first of all, I want to thank you for your comments on my speech, and I am very pleased to see that the Chair agrees with me.
If I understood his comments correctly, it was mainly about what we would do if we were in power. Well, in 1992, I will show you exactly what we will do.
Hear, hear.
Oh, oh!

Meanwhile- Would you please have the courtesy to hear me out? If I were the Minister, I would not have cut off transfer payments. I would not have cut training and skills upgrading. I would have increased funding for research and development. I would have increased financial support for literacy training. Those are some of things that could have been done. I would have- I must say that the Minister is very good at putting the blame on the Opposition. He is always saying: "It's the Liberal's fault! It's the Liberals fault! What would you have done if you were in power?" I told you what I would do. If you wish, I can give a few more examples. If I were you, I would stop claiming that these cutbacks have had no negative impact on our competitive position, on our Canadian identity, on youth, on Canadians, on Native people, on women, on our young men and women. I would tell the truth!
Hear, hear.
Madam Speaker, I consider very unfortunate what has happened in the House in the last five to ten minutes.
Order.

I think my hon. friend from St. Boniface gave a very thoughtful presentation. I congratulate him on what he has said in this House. I think it is very unfortunate that a Minister would inject such irresponsible and foolish remarks as he has done in the past few minutes.
Order.

I do have a question, Madam Speaker. I am not going to ramble on with a silly presentation as did the Minister. I have a question for the Hon. Member for St. Boniface. It concerns his remarks when he said that there was a mounting debt on the part of students in this country and that there was an increase in tuition fees.
My question is simply this: As a result of mounting debt and increased tuition fees, does he see the possibility of some students either having to quit university because of the situation or some students not being able to go to university because they simply cannot afford it?

Yes, I do foresee that possibility. In fact, there are a number of documented cases which show that students have not been able to go to college or university. A number of documented cases show that they have been unable to continue because of the lack of financial assistance.
There is no question that unless things are changed in a dramatic kind of way the situation will get worse, not better. This is the cause of a great deal of sadness about which everyone agrees. When are we going to do something about it?
Unless our post-secondary institutions and all services related to them are improved in a significant and substantial way, we will lose our competitiveness. We will no longer have Canadians believing that they can become educated and carve out an important niche for themselves, especially in terms of participating in the democratic process, in finding a job, and in contributing to their communities. That feeling is starting and in fact has been running for some time now. It is getting worse.
We need to provide the resources so that more Canadians can participate, particularly under-represented groups. Once they are there participating they need to have the resources and the supports in place so that they continue their programs of training.

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate today and to discuss the motion of the Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duhamel). He has indeed addressed some very important issues. In fact, any one of the issues that he has mentioned could take
June 13, 1989

up a full day's debate in this House. We would probably need more time even after that.
We on this side of the House are aware, as perhaps members of the Opposition are not, of the Government's achievements in terms of science and technology. I think it might be useful if we were to review in some detail, for their benefit, exactly what we have done. I will restrict my remarks pretty much to science and technology, with perhaps a few remarks dealing with the post-secondary education issue. My colleagues will cover the other issues such as training and retraining, the battle against illiteracy, and post-secondary education in general.

Madam Speaker, if any government ever recognized the importance of scientific and technological development, it certainly is this one! This Government and its Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) are very much aware of the impact it will have on the Canada of tomorrow.

Long before he entered politics the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was an outspoken advocate for the need to hone our competitive edge in industries by increasing the amount of science and technology not only in the country but in industry in particular-
That is why you shut down the steel plants.

I thank the Hon. Member for his courtesy. After becoming Prime Minister he chaired, and continues to chair, the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology which has provided the Government with some significant advice. That board involves people from business, academe, government, labour, and the scientific community in general. It is as I know-and I have met with them several times-a very powerful board.
Just last evening I met with the steering committee of the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology to discuss new ways in which we could make Canada competitive and the kinds of things that the board should take under its wing for the next year, along the lines of what the Hon. Member for St. Boniface has been talking about. The National Advisory Board will continue to assess our national goals, our policies for science and
Supply
technology, and their application to industry competitiveness in the country, which is an extremely important point.
The Prime Minister, as Members of the House know, has also altered Cabinet to reflect the new emphasis on high technology and the developing technologies. In fact, the enabling legislation for the new Department of Industry, Science and Technology is now before this House. I believe, as we just heard, it cleared the legislative committee last night. Perhaps the House will dispose of it on third reading rather quickly.
The new Department will be the flagship economic policy Department that will link industry with science and technology, trying to move ahead significantly in terms of our industrial capacity and our ability to compete.
As well, the Government has participated in the Council of Science and Technology Ministers. We have been strongly supportive of the previous House of Commons Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology. We now intend to be supportive of the new House of Commons Standing Committee on Industry, Science and Technology.
We have been building a consensus while we have been developing a comprehensive science and technology policy for Canada through such things as the Forum for National Science and Technology which was held in Toronto, the National Forum on Post-Secondary Education held in Saskatoon, and the National Conference on Technology and Innovation. All those things go toward trying to form a consensus in the country and an awareness of where we have to go. We have consulted widely. We have established a solid framework to revitalize science and technology in the country.
The programs that we have implemented or, indeed, are implementing are a result of consultation and collaboration. They are among some of the most advanced programs anywhere in the world as we try to move toward the end that the Hon. Member for St. Boniface is encouraging upon us.
As usual, I think Members opposite do not think we have gone far enough. They insist that we have not spent enough on science and technology. They suggest that we spend more and more government money, that is, on science and technology. Next week they will be suggest-

June 13, 1989
Supply
ing in one of their motions that we spend money on other things.
Members opposite are indeed in an enviable position. They can dream of spending their imaginary dollars over and over again while we, unfortunately or fortunately for the country, have to make the hard choices with limited resources. I often think what we could do if we were not saddled with the debt that came out of 20 years of Liberal Government. Just think what we could do with that $39 billion interest. That is 70 times the amount of money we can put into the granting councils.
We recognize that we have to be judicious in spending taxpayers' money.
When are you going to start?

We also know that funding is crucial to the science and technology programs of the country.
I recall the words of a famous Nobel laureate who said that research is four things: brains with which to think, eyes with which to see, machines with which to measure, and money. The Government has responded to that need for research through a series of well targeted programs.
Some of those programs make a direct contribution to university research. At the opening of the National Conference on Technology and Innovation last year the Prime Minister announced that $1.3 billion would be made available for science and technology, new initiatives that is, over the next five years. That funding is broken down into a number of programs. One of the programs which I understand has received universal acclaim across the country and has received the support of my colleagues on the opposition benches is the Canada Scholarship Program under which $80 million will be used to encourage outstanding secondary school graduates to pursue undergraduate studies in natural sciences, engineering and related disciplines. When that program reaches fruition, there will be 10,000 young men and women who are Canada scholars. That is a pretty good beginning.
A year ago last May, the details of a $240 million five-year program to establish the National Centres of Excellence was announced. The program will promote university-industry partnerships to enhance world class research and to promote Canada's competitive position.
It is important for Hon. Members to know that that program is a university led program. The main participants in the consortia will be universities with support from Government laboratories and, of course, industry. It will be mostly university led.
At the same time as we announced that program, the Government increased the base budgets of the three granting councils by $200 million over that same period. I remind Hon. Members that the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Medical Research Council and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council will also administer the budgets for the Networks of Centres of Excellence. Not only will they have their own program of distributing funds to university researchers, but they will be the main operators in terms of the peer review of the national networks of excellence.
The financial impact of these programs is really quite substantial. The Government has provided over half a billion dollars to the funding available for university research and training of highly qualified personnel over the next five years. When that is added to the contributions we anticipate from the private sector through the matching policy which was announced in the Budget of February, 1986, we expect over the next five years a full $3.7 billion for university research and training of scientists and engineers.
I think it is clear to Hon. Members that the Government is working very hard indeed to ensure that science and technology is supported in post-secondary institutions. Looking at what governments alone do in terms of supporting basic research, particularly in the academic area, Canada does not stack up too badly. We do quite well.
Hon. Members would not expect me to hold the position I hold in this Government if I were not constantly badgering you, Madam Speaker, and all my other colleagues for more funding for science and technology, and that is important. Even more important is to somehow ensure that whatever funding is available to Government is used to help promote the industrial research and development that Canada so badly needs. That is the real emphasis.
Through the strategic technologies program, we are again trying to forge alliances, this time led by industry. These will be alliances of industries coming together
June 13, 1989

with universities and government to form that pre-competitive atmosphere that is so necessary to move ahead.
In the new competitive environment we see all around us today, many companies that have never done research before will have to do research. We will have to encourage that through the formation of these alliances that will bring small companies together with larger companies or groups of small companies together with Government labs and universities. These alliances will promote the concept of doing research in Canadian industry.
Let me talk for just a moment about federal transfers to the provinces. When most Hon. Members talk about that, they try to make a simple issue out of a very complex situation. We have increased funding to Canadian post-secondary institutions from something like $3.3 billion in 1981-1982 to $5.7 billion now. As part of our effort to reduce Canada's staggering debt, we have reduced the rate of growth of EPF transfers by one percentage point beginning in 1991. However, these transfers will continue to grow at the rate of inflation as a minimum, and as Hon. Members know, the transfers are provided so that the provinces can give grants to universities to cover capital and operating expenditures. There is a catch, though. We have no way of knowing or ensuring that the money we give to the provinces is used for the purpose for which it was intended. Do opposition Members really believe that post-secondary education is the sole responsibility of the federal Government?
We haven't said that.

They say yes. We are having a marvellous debate.

I would like to know what the Opposition has to suggest to ensure that transfer payments reach their destination: our universities.

Would they favour earmarking funds? There are implications to that. Would they prefer to give the EPF money to the granting councils and have them take over the whole responsibility for administering research in Canada at the post-secondary level? Would they prefer to leave the funds in the hands of the provinces entirely? How would they guarantee that other provincial funds
Supply
would not be transferred away from post-secondary education if our funds were earmarked for post-secondary education? Those are important questions, questions that simply cannot be sloughed off. Those are questions that require some serious debate around the table. That is what we need to do.
When are you going to start?

Oh, we have started.

Madam Speaker, the Opposition seems to have some very specific ideas about what it does not like about our funding policy. Perhaps it could share some concrete suggestions with us.

I wish we had more time to sit down and have a serious debate-
Not if that is all you have to say.

Interesting. I wish we had more time to sit down and have a serious debate on the development of science and technology in Canada. We will hear later about the initiatives the Government has undertaken in such areas as job training and literacy as well as the broader question of post-secondary education.
I think it should be clear to all Hon. Members that when it comes to providing, in the words of the motion, the essential foundation for building a strong and competitive future for Canada, the Government's record has been pointing entirely in the right direction. I would like to conclude by saying two things. In my opinion, there are two issues that will prevent Canada from being competitive. I have said before that we pride ourselves on being a caring society. If we want to continue being a caring society we must, of course, be a competitive society. There are two things that will prevent that. First, the failure to take action on the ball and chain that each of us drags across the floor, the national debt and the growing interest rates. We must tackle that.
Second, we must, through the use of the kinds of programs that I have been talking about, bring industry in total, not just a few in the high tech area, into doing research and development so that we can proceed, meet

Supply
the global competition and continue to have the kind of Canada that we all want.

Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Minister on his thoughtful speech on these important topics. He has raised a few points upon which I would like to comment and finally a point on which I would like to direct a question.
He spoke about the national debt, and the need to increase our spending being limited by our ability to cope with the debt problem. It is important to note that in the context of the national debt the Prime Minister did make an announcement a year or so ago of increasing new spending on science and technology by $1.3 billion. We have tried our best to find out where that $1.3 billion is being spent. Notwithstanding remarks by a previous Minister that it was not going into the space program, we find that some of it is. We find that $525 million of it is going into the Department of Industry, Science and Technology with no assurance that it is going to be new money.
I think it is important for this Minister of State, in particular, to recognize the fact that when we are talking about science and technology we are not talking about spending programs per se, we are talking about investments, investments that if they are not made are going to cost us far more in the long run.
The Minister has talked with some pride about the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology, and justifiably so, because this is a panel of some of the best people in Canada. Their advice to the Government is well worth while. This board advised the Government in its report published a year or so ago that the federal Government "double the budgets of the three granting councils over the following three years. Subsequent budgets should grow at an annual rate of one and half times the rate of GNP growth." Governments ignored this recommendation, Madam Speaker. I wonder why we bother bringing these significant minds together to give advice which is ignored.
In fact most of the additional funding has come to the granting councils through the matching grants program which is very unreliable because it depends upon money being contributed to the universities by the private
sector, out of the control of the granting councils altogether.
It talks about the Canada scholarship program. As late as March of this year students were still waiting for some of their payments from the Canada scholarship program. This is a great idea but it would be nice to get the cash before the school year is over.
The Minister has talked about the Department of Industry, Science and Technology as the flagship economic policy department. I quote: "We on this side have sought to have as part of the objectives of that Department included in its mandate in legislation concern for environmentally sustainable development exactly in line with the recommendations of the Brundtland Commission. This is the key to our advance as a nation and to our survival that we tie all economic development to the needs of the environment." I would like to know why, in the Minister's opinion, his Government is unwilling to tie as an objective of the Department of Industry, Science and Technology environmentally sustainable development.

Madam Speaker, the Member really had several questions but I will try to respond to them all. First, the Hon. Member suggested that he has not seen the $1.3 billion. I assure him that it is still there. In fact, he gave some of the figures himself, the $80 million for the Canada Scholarships Program, $200 million for the granting councils, $240 million for the Centres of Excellence Program, the space science program and some $500 million for industry, science and technology which we are going to use for R and D. Out of those funds comes the strategic technology program which, indeed, is one of the programs that I think has the ability to do a great deal for the country. So, the money is there.
I come to NABST, the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology. When one has a national board or any kind of senior advisory council one tries to pay a great deal of attention to it, but that does not mean that one can meet every recommendation. That is a false impression of how Government responds to advice. It gets the advice and does its best to meet that but has to work it into its other priorities. NABST itself is quite content with the work it is doing, the advice it gives and the general Government response it receives.
June 13, 1989

In coming to the environment, I think the answer to the question is that one of the Ministers of the Department sits on the Environment Committee of Cabinet. So, all of the issues that go through the main program come before that environmental committee of Cabinet and it is deliberate that one of the Ministers sits on that committee.

Madam Speaker, I would like to comment on the Minister's speech and perhaps ask him for a comment. I note that the debate today is being carried by people who were not here during the last Government. These new Members ask that the Government spend money to achieve the objectives of post-secondary education and scientific and technological development.
I want to cite an example that occurred during the last Government when it amended the Patent Act under Bill C-22. Under previous laws, drug companies in Canada were subject to copy in as little as four years after they applied to have their drug licensed in Canada to the point where they were withdrawing drugs from the market-I hope that is a fair statement-or delaying their introduction to the point that they were reducing the amount of research done in Canada. I want to say to the new Members and to the Minister that I believe there is a way of stimulating all of the things stated in the motion of the Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duhamel) other than the government spending of money.
I wonder if the Minister would care to comment on policies other than the spending of money that have done all of the things that motion asks us to do.

Madam Speaker, I believe the point is very well taken. Bill C-22 was a good example. In fact, I am trying to be generous in the spirit of this debate because I think it should not be a raucous issue.
I believe it was the Hon. Member for Ottawa South who raised the issue the other day about the difficulty with certain tax measures which prevented consortia from operating in the manner in which we would like them to operate. That is helpful when we know these things so that we can try to resolve those issues and push ahead. It does not require the Government to put up more money. It requires the Government to do something reasonable to promote R and D. Those are the
Supply
kinds of issues that I believe we could all look at and make some headway.
I also want to take up the point again about using government money to lever other issues in these alliances. I remind the House that two or three weeks ago I signed an agreement for something I call "smart speakers"-not you, Madam Speaker, we recognize that is always the case-for five small companies that are working and coming together with funding from the National Research Council, and their own money, to develop a research program to produce these smart speakers that would recognize what was in the way and change the sound patterns. That type of alliance where we lever something outside is our only hope. We do not have billions of dollars to throw at any problem any more.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Regina-Qu'Appelle.

Madam Speaker, I too wish to join in the debate this morning on the opposition motion presented by the Liberal Party which calls for a greater and enhanced federal commitment to the support of post-secondary education, scientific and technological development, job training and retraining and the battle against illiteracy.
Previous speakers from both the government and the opposition Parties have indicated the importance of scientific research and development if Canada is to remain competitive, if we are to be able to fulfil our destiny, and explore the many opportunities that modem life has to offer to our citizens.
We all recognize the importance of moving away from a resource-based economy and society to a knowledge-based society. If we are to remain competitive in terms of international trade, if we are to be able to provide meaningful jobs to our men and women and to the young students who are now in high schools and universities, if we are to be able to provide a sense of opportunity, future and hope to the citizens of Canada, we must remain competitive and we must invest more in terms of research and development. We must correct the wrongs that have been committed by past Liberal Governments and by the present Conservative Government. I suspect if we put our partisanship aside, every Member of the House will admit that we have not done enough as a

June 13, 1989
Supply
country to ensure that we have a vibrant and healthy research and development component in our country today.
Let us stop for a moment and look at the statistics and what is happening in our universities. In our major universities the library facilities are inadequate. Scientists, professors, and administrators in major universities have explained and described to us the conditions of laboratories and equipment. Much of the equipment in laboratories is totally outdated. In some facilities walls are crumbling and paint is dropping down. At times we have heard reports of dead rats and mice being found in the laboratories of our universities. That is totally inadequate. The equipment is totally inadequate.
In terms of human resources in our universities and research facilities there is a total lack of support staff. The number of students per professor has increased over the years. Over the last number of years we have seen the research capacity in our universities slowly but steadily degrade. We have also seen rising costs to our university students. As the cost of educating our young people increases, the universities have responded by increasing tuition fees and at the same time making it more difficult for students to enter by increasing the qualifications.
The danger is that universities will only become accessible to a very few. There is a dangerous trend setting in that takes away from the egalitarian notion that has guided post-secondary education in Canada for many years. This of course works against women. Historically, our universities have been slanted towards men. The university population has generally been more male than female. Over the last number of years this trend started to be corrected. I suggest that the more difficult it becomes to gain entrance into a university, again we will see discrimination against females. Restricting accessibility to universities will hurt the number of women and the opportunities that they will have to enter university.
Over the last number of years student support programs have gone downwards. Bursaries and scholarships are available to only a few. Many students are dependent upon loans which can burden them with a huge debt load, as much as $35,000 upon graduation. Part-time students, especially women, face severe barriers such as a $2,500 loan limit and a requirement that payment begin
six months after graduation. Both the facilities at universities and the support programs for students and graduate students are being diminished.
Surely that is a responsibility the present Conservative Government must share in. This is despite what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) originally stated when he was in Opposition.
I am certain the following quote has been put on the record many times, but it is worth repeating. In a book the Prime Minister wrote entitled Where I Stand he stated: "The starting line for me is the technological dimension. Either we go into the game and become important players in the major leagues or we become a nation that will, in its entire lifetime, play in the Junior B circuit". This was written by the Prime Minister on Canada's poor performance in science and technology.
Yet, what is the record? In terms of the EPF programs we see in this particular Budget a further cut-back. Less money will be going to the provinces for Established Programs Financing.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: Less money?
More money will be going to the provinces.
We hear now from the Conservatives. The line being proposed is that they are not cutting back the amount of money that will be going to the provinces and therefore to the universities.
There will be $25 million more in the next five years.

What is occurring is that the increase in terms of inflation and in terms of needs will not be the same as was the previous program. The universities will see less money than they would have under the previous program. This occurred when the Tories first introduced their cuts in the 1985-86 Budget. When the Liberals did it in 1982, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), then in opposition, stated on February 1, 1982:
The Minister is proposing to cut spending in two very important areas. He is prepared to risk major cut-backs in medical care and post-secondary education. Rather than rush into this on a unilateral basis and force spending cuts and service cuts on the provinces, would the minister and the government consider entering into two or three national conferences on health and post-secondary education so that we can set out the national objectives of the various levels of government in these two important areas before we cut
June 13, 1989

spending, and before we cause closures of hospitals and cut-backs in post-secondary education?
That was stated by the Minister of Finance when he was in opposition on February 1, 1982. When the Liberals did it, the Tories said that it was a cut-back. Now that the Tories are doing exactly the same thing, it is not a cut-back, and to the Liberals it has become a cut-back.
The fact of the matter is that under both Liberal and Conservative Governments there have been cut-backs to post-secondary education and to our health programs. When the Liberals did it, the Tories accused the Liberals of cutting back on post-secondary education and on health care. The Government of the day, the Liberals, said: "No, these are programs the provincial Governments can spend as they wish and therefore we are not forcing a cut-back on post-secondary education and on health care." Now that we see the reversal with the Tories in government, they are claiming that it is not a cut-back to post-secondary education.
We are now hearing the Liberals make the charge that the Tories used to make when they were in opposition. One must ask: Where is the commitment? The commitment only exists when these Parties are in opposition. When they are in government, they lose their commitment.
We must also examine the Liberal commitment to science and technology. In opposition they proposed that the expenditures on R and D should be 2.5 per cent of our Gross Domestic Product. When they were in power they consistently fell below that. In the 1984 election they were to introduce a quick fix. They introduced a tax proposal, namely, the scientific research tax credit. That particular proposal blew around $2 billion of taxpayers' money with very little research and development to show for it. The only R and D that came out of that proposal was R and D by smart tax accountants who figured out ways and means of saving companies tax moneys or perpetuating tremendous tax scams.
I hear Liberal Members suggesting that I am exaggerating. Let me tell them that the SRTC tax scam was one of the most major tax scams in the history of this country. It was a badly thought through proposal and wasted much money. If that $2 billion been used for genuine research and development, we would have seen universi-
Supply
ties in a much different situation from the one they are in today. However, the Conservatives should not take too much credit in terms of closing down that tax scheme. It was introduced in the spring of 1984. We warned that it was a tax scam, that it was not going to produce any research and development.
The Tories were elected in the fall of 1984, but did they close the tax scam down? No, they did not. It took them until May of the following year finally to close it down. Half of what was lost in terms of revenue was lost in the period of time between the election of the Conservative Government and when they finally closed it down. They should have closed it down right after the election. They knew it was a tax scam. They knew what was being lost under that particular scheme.
What the scientific research tax credit scam shows, and the difficulty we faced in terms of scientific research and development under Liberal and Conservative Governments, is really a lack of a systematic plan to tie in our economic development with an economic strategy and a social strategy. We must tie in our economic strategy with what we spend on research and development through our universities, through our various scientific institutions. What is so desperately needed is a strategy that will begin to target key sectors of the economy, to channel our financial resources, technological resources, and various public and private resources to ensure that as a country we become number one in those particular areas.
That is what the Europeans are doing with the European Economic Community. That is what the Japanese have done. That is what these countries have done, and they have become very successful in developing their research and development. Unfortunately in this country, we still continue to follow a helter-skelter strategy. We lose money and very often we waste money on research and development. It has resulted in Canada being eighth among the OECD countries in terms of what we spend on research and development as a percentage of our Gross Domestic Product.
Let us look at the history of research and development in Canada compared to Sweden. Sweden is a small country. In fact it is smaller than Canada in terms of population. Yet, what it spent as a percentage of its Gross Domestic Product on research and development between 1971 and 1986 ranged between 1.5 per cent and

Supply
2.5 per cent, compared to Canada's record of around 1.4 per cent of our Gross Domestic Product.
In terms of developing high-tech industry, the Swedes have become veiy successful. They have done it as part of an industrial strategy. In Sweden it is the trade union movement that is in the forefront of technological change. When the price of oil went up in 1973, the Swedish unions recognized that unless Swedish industry became competitive and increased its efficiency, they were going to be priced out of the world market.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: Explain that to Shirley.

Let me make my point here. The Tories are always anxious to bring up Shirley Carr. Let me finish making my point.
The trade union movement in Sweden has scientists on its staff who know the most up to date technologies in the world. In Sweden the Government, the unions, and the private industry work together to ensure that Swedish industry is one of the most competitive in the world. That is why I can go down to Ikea and buy a table costing $75 that is made in Sweden with Swedish softwood, shipped over here, and sold in that store. They are able to accomplish that efficiency because they have a mixed economy. There is a social contract among labour, business, and government.
It means that when Swedish industry makes money because of new technological innovations, it reinvests it in Sweden and in Swedish industry. Union contracts ensure that there will be reinvestment in the plant and equipment and that there will be research and development done in Sweden. They also ensure that there is a social net to retrain Swedish workers who may lose their jobs because of technological innovation. It ensures that they will not lose their mortgages and will not see a decline in their living standards. They will be fully consulted in the implementation of that new technology. That is the smart way to introduce science and new technology, in a co-operative way among workers, business, and government.
In Canada-and here I come back to my Conservative friends-working people are afraid of research and development and new technologies because they know there is no retraining program. They are afraid because, if they lose their jobs, they will lose their mortgages,
their standard of living, and they will slide on unemployment down to the welfare level. That is the concern and the legitimate fear of working men and women in this country. Unless the Government stops attacking our social system, there will be resistance by working people against scientific research and technological innovations. Very rightly and legitimately working people are afraid of losing their jobs, their mortgages, and their standard of living.
If we are to have an efficient Canadian industry with high paying jobs, which the Swedes are able to do, we must develop a contract, a social understanding, among labour, government, and industry. This would mean that all sectors of our society could begin to act responsibly. The Tories are the first in line to denounce labour for acting irresponsibly. I suggest to them that they act irresponsibly when the Government starts cutting back on EPF, cutting back on retraining programs, not fulfilling its promises about day care, and starting to cut the social net which reassures working men and women that they will not lose their standard of living as a result of technological innovations.
Social responsibility requires that when industrial profits rise there is a commitment to keep those profits in Canada by reinvesting in research and development and new technologies.
One reason that Canada has such a low percentage of research and development as part of its Gross Domestic Product is that private industry does not do research and development in this country. Another reason for such a dismal record of R and D investment in Canada is that most of our industries are foreign controlled. Companies in a branch plant economy do not do research and development here but in their home countries. I am not saying anything new. The Lafontaine committee set up by the Liberals many years ago pointed that out as well.
Yet the Liberals, during their term in office, failed to make certain that Canadian industry was controlled by Canadians. The Liberals allowed the multinationals to come in and buy us up. It was the defeat of Walter Gordon and the fight within the Liberal Party that led to the lost opportunity of making certain that Canadian industries would be owned by Canadians. We are now
June 13, 1989

seeing some of the results of Liberal policies of the 1950s and 1960s-
Supported by the NDP.

I will forget that comment because it is not made on the basis of intelligence or reason.
The fact that we are essentially a branch plant economy means that there has been low research and development investment here by industries. Consequently, we do not have the jobs for our young technologists and scientists. This has to be blamed initially on the Liberals, and certainly the Tories are finishing off the job as they sell us into the arms of the multinationals. There must be increased research and development. In order to achieve that, many changes will have to be made.

Madam Speaker, I want to correct the Hon. Member. I understand that all of us are ignorant in different areas, and the Hon. Member has perhaps reached into an area about which he is somewhat ignorant. What he said about Ikea and the Swedish innovative way of manufacturing low cost furniture was true a couple or three years ago when the Liberal policies were still flourishing. It is not true today.
There are several plants that have perfected the Ikea idea and are manufacturing furniture with Canadian pine lumber and Canadian workers, not just for the Canadian domestic market but for export of that particular furniture. His statement that we are importing a Swedish idea and Swedish pine wood to Canada is no longer true. We corrected that.
I was intrigued by his suggestion that it is the Government's fault and industry's fault that there is little or few opportunities for young Canadians to take apprenticeship training to upgrade their skills. He laments the fact that there is not the kind of partnership in terms of the industrial relations process that exists in countries like Sweden and Germany.
I suggest to him that the unions deserve a little bit of the blame for that because they prefer the adversarial system that is the fundamental nature and main element of our industrial process. It is the unions that resist young people being allowed to come into a company to learn a trade and perhaps get a lesser wage while they are doing it. It is the unions that resist the introduction of new technology in plants because they are afraid of
Supply
their jobs. While I readily admit that others are to blame, generally speaking it is the unions that resist it.
If the Member wants to use the Swedish model, perhaps he will recognize that the unions in Sweden encourage their employers to establish plants in other parts of the world so that their ideas will reach out and the workers can secure their jobs at home. There is a totally different attitude to labour in countries like Sweden, Germany, and Japan.
If he wants to do this country a favour he should talk to his friends in the union movement, take them to Sweden to look at those models, and try to implement them here. It is quite true that unions in Sweden have scientists on their staff. As well, the best economists in countries like Germany also work for the union movement. Our unions are not interested in that. They prefer the adversarial process in which they are right and everyone else is wrong. The Hon. Member actually believes that.

Madam Speaker, it is interesting to hear the Member, a former Minister of State for Science and Technology. He has made two points. One is that because of his Government's policies Swedish pine furniture is no longer coming into Canada and the other is that Canadian companies have followed the Swedish technology and have become so competitive that there is no need to import Swedish pine furniture. I must tell the Hon. Member that just a few weeks ago I was at the Ikea store where it was plum full of pine furniture from Sweden that seems to be selling quite well. I am not suggesting that there are not Canadian companies which are able to compete.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: It is made in Canada. Ikea is contracting to make it in Canada. You are missing the point.

Perhaps I could finish my remarks. The other point made by the Hon. Member is more serious. He reverts to pointing to the unions as the real reason that we do not have the technological innovations. He suggests that their resistance is the cause of the bottleneck to technological innovations in this country. He then compared us to the Swedes.
The Member still has not understood the point I was making. I said that the reason Canadian workers are afraid of technological change, as opposed to Swedish workers, is that there is no social guarantee in this country. During the last election I sat with a man in his fifties who was a pipe fitter. He was in tears because his traditional job had been wiped out. He had been unemployed for six or seven months and recognized that his

June 13, 1989
Supply
future was just a downward slide to the rolls of the unemployed, with no future. It is no wonder that working people fight tooth and nail against that.
If the Government begins to offer working people a guarantee that they will be retrained and there will not be a decrease in their standard of living, they would be in the forefront of technological change. They will help introduce new technological changes. They will want newer, better reforms of production to make certain there are good wages in their industry and to ensure that their industry is competitive on a world-wide basis. They will want to make certain that when the new technologies are introduced their work will become more pleasant and less dehumanizing.
Working people will become involved with technological innovation when they are given that assurance. It is the irresponsibility of the Government and its attack on our social programs that create fear among working people.

Madam Speaker, when we initiated this discussion I had hoped that we might collectively attempt to identify certain problems and perhaps address those issues to see what we might do for those who are not participating fully in education-the poor, a number of women, native people, a number of new Canadians, and people from smaller, more isolated regions. While some important points have been made, I bristled a bit when a member of the Government suggested more than once that we were somewhat irresponsible spenders and that we did not care about the deficit. He accused us of having accumulated a lot of debt.
If that kind of discussion continues, we are going to get away from the main thrust. I would hope that somehow the Government would see fit to admit that it has in fact doubled that debt in the last five years. Perhaps the blame should be shared.
The major focus of the Hon. Member appears to have been, in spite of the fact that he set partisanship aside, on the errors of the Liberals of the past and the Conservatives of present. I would suggest that our focus
on what is happening now to try to bring about responsible solutions might be much more productive.
I would like to ask the Member this very brief question. He has referred to the errors of previous Liberal administrations and current Conservative administrations. There has been a number of New Democratic Governments in power. I wonder if he would care to comment about their records in the administration of funding for education. Just in case he is not familiar with the details, I would be more than willing to provide some.

Madam Speaker, I do not have the statistics at my fingertips on what New Democratic Party Governments, when we were in government in B.C., in Manitoba, or in Saskatchewan, spent on education. Of course we want to put it into the context of increases over a number of years.
I know, just in terms of my own personal experience, in Saskatchewan, that during the Douglas Government and the Blakeney Government university funding was increased over the years, but certainly not as much as I would have liked. I remember, when I was president of the students' council in 1963-64, leading the students out on strike against the Lloyd Government which was cutting back on university funding and resulting in an increase in student fees.
I feel that no Government has really spent the type of money and provided the investment in our post-secondary education which I think it deserves. It is an investment in the future. I think the Government is making a mistake. It might save pennies, but it is going to cost dollars in the long run. We can cut back on education and programs which do away with illiteracy, but we are going to pay for it. We are going to pay for it in higher social costs over the years. An educated population results in better paying jobs, which result in higher revenues for the Governments and for the public purse. I suggest that investments in education and in science and technology pay back many, many fold in the long run.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, some time ago, a new provision that would apply on Opposition days, when the House considers an Opposition motion, was adopted unanimously by the House. Each political party may divide the twenty-minute period for speeches plus ten minutes for questions and comments in two equal periods of ten minutes, each followed by a five-minute period for questions and comments.
I would like to suggest the following, today, now we have had our first round. Each Party representative has had a chance to speak his twenty minutes plus ten. We of the Liberal Party would like to suggest to the House that Hon. Members adopt a procedure by which from now on, each Party, when its turn is called, may divide the conventional twenty minutes into two ten-minute periods, each followed by five minutes of questions and comments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we on the government side have co-operated in terms of this procedure in the past. We believe that it is a good one and want to co-operate again today.
I would indicate, though, that we do have two speakers left who I understand will probably want to use the full 20 minutes. Certainly we have no problems with the spirit of that. As the Parties are ready to split their speeches I think it is a good idea, and also to have the time period for questions split as well.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There seems to be unanimous consent.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Halifax.

Madam Speaker, the fate of the universities in this country hangs in the balance following the budget cuts to established program funding. Most particularly the fate of universities in Atlantic Canada are in a precarious state. My riding of Halifax has seven universities, each with a unique role to play. Universities are fragile and complex institutions. They are the repositories of accumulated knowledge of our civilization. They are the foster parents of the future.
Universities are, it is true, only one of the elements in the tertiary educational system. Community colleges, apprenticeship, and vocational certification programs are the others. Universities are the pathfinders of the
Supply
societal change in every sense of that concept. Today, technology is the chic word but political, social, economic and cultural change will be forgotten only to our peril. In Canada we have evolved a university system which integrates traditions of European and North American education.
One has only to travel to developing nations to understand what a tremendous resource we have. Sadly we have managed to allow the potential of our universities to become the victim of shortsighted political concerns. Differential fees for foreign students and our failure to market our universities internationally have seriously diminished the capacity of universities to build global links which could be of immense future importance.
Canadian embassies are reticent to enter into what is considered provincial competition for foreign students and thus will often not market Canadian universities. Historically in this country we have education as a national social priority; thus the established program funding system which is an hybrid offshoot of the original notion of equalization positive in the Act of Confederation.
What complicates this system is the relationship of the division of powers as stated in the BNA Act and the principles of equalization as they evolved in the 20th century. Spheres of influence tended to muddy the waters of 20th century social policy. The debates over transfer payments and the evolution of the EPF system are marvellous case studies of the adaptation of 19th century concepts, often fuzzy and ill-developed as was appropriate to that time, to 20th century policy imperatives. Much can be said about this point.
With respect to the fundamental role of universities, the evolution of EPF and the decision to integrate tertiary education into the equalization game have had some dire consequences for the quality of education. It is wise not to romanticize equalization, for it really is premised upon the concept of the lowest common denominator.
Philosophically EPF guarantees minimum standards rather than creating maximum goals. In financial terms this has specific results. The federal Government transfers funds, and the provincial Government, quite properly, decides upon their allocation. It can be argued that there is no answer to this, other than a responsible and

June 13, 1989
co-operative collaboration between the two levels of government.
The financial commitment to the support of post-secondary education cannot in our constitutional picture be viewed as a back door to altering the established relationship of federal and provincial powers. The time has come for change, a change which is so desperately needed in the universities of this country. It must be through co-operative and sensitive federal-provincial negotiations.
The federal Government has chosen a more subtle route to amending the existing system. Having recognized that a national policy on education-and the very term is fraught with unwanted images-is a political minefield, the Government has de-indexed and done other cute financial things to EPF funding for education. The result is a very tragic one.
