Mr. Speaker, the acid rain proposal by President Bush will cost American utilities an estimated $700 million per year, or half the cost of a Trident submarine, to achieve only a 42 per cent reduction of pollution by the year 2000. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) likes this proposal and claims that by 1995 our lakes and forests will come back to life. Unfortunately, he is naive.
Canada should have at least two major concerns with President Bush's proposal. The plan appears to allow juggling because of the trading provisions for polluters.
There is the possibility that the big polluters who dump on Canada will trade for the right to continue polluting instead of making cuts.
Second, there is no cap on emissions. As the American economy grows, the allowable pollution would grow even though new sources would meet the emission standards. President Bush's proposal does not ensure that the health of our rivers, forests, buildings and structures will be protected. We urge the Government to ensure that Congress shortens the deadlines, raises the targets and caps the emissions.

Mr. Speaker, get this. The NDP wants to try and run a squeaky clean leadership campaign. Now, that is highly unlikely. This MP from Churchill says, "We're not going to try and use the tax system". Well, Mr. Speaker, why should they change now? Remember how this present Leader wrote to business Canadians using his government frank to solicit funds? The Churchill MP also says, "We cannot be seen as using House of Commons facilities". My NDP office neighbour from the last Parliament ran the entire maritime campaign from a Parliament Hill suite.
Canadians will also remember that this squeaky clean Party had the policy of using federal funds to finance municipal New Democrat politicians. Clearly, the NDP should look beyond this House for someone eligible to strut their squeaky clean stuff.

subtopic: DONATION TO HELP PAY OFF NATIONAL DEBT
DONATION TO HELP PAY OFF NATIONAL DEBT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Reverend Seymour Boyce and Mr. Allan Tobey, layman in charge, and the congregation of the British Methodist Episcopal Church of Canada, Owen Sound, Ontario, have indeed the concern, the love and the welfare of our country uppermost in their minds.
Encouraged by the action of a Canadian lady who a few weeks ago presented a cheque to her MP to help pay off the debt, they presented me with a cheque of $100 to be presented to you, Mr. Speaker, to forward on to the

Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to be used to help defray our national debt.
Hopefully, the example of this unselfish deed will gather momentum all across our country and, who knows, perhaps we will be paying off our national debt sooner than expected.
As well, all donations to Governments are 100 per cent deductible.

Mr. Speaker, this week is Spina Bifida Week across Canada. It is a time for all Canadians to examine the realities associated with spina bifida and the related condition, hydrocephalus. Spina bifida is the most common disabling birth defect in Canada. It affects more children than muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, multiple sclerosis and polio combined.
To raise the profile of spina bifida and in honour of Spina Bifida Week, I have spent the day with Sue Mackay who was bom with this disease. Sue joins us this afternoon in the gallery. Her courage in performing the every day chores and duties that most of us take for granted is an inspiration for me and for all Canadians.
As little as 30 years ago, the majority of children bom with this congenital defect died of complications. Now with aggressive up-to-date medical and surgical care, at least 90 per cent of people with spina bifida live and lead full and productive lives.
I call on my colleagues in this House and all Canadians to consider the importance of research and treatment of spina bifida and hydrocephalus and to recognize the personal victories of the Sue Mackays of this world.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, this Government claims the letting of government contracts is done in a fair and equitable manner. Yet the Government is the victim of its own statistics.
A recent report from the Canadian Government Printing Services Branch shows that 89.2 per cent of government printing contracts go to Ontario and Quebec, home of only 63.5 per cent of workers; 10.7 per cent goes to the four western provinces, home to 28.8 per cent of Canadian workers; and .01 per cent goes to Atlantic Canada, home of 7.7 per cent of workers. My home province of British Columbia received only 1.2 per cent of contracts with a work force of 15.2 per cent.
The printing industry is on the sacrificial altar of free trade and will not survive if the Government continues such blatant discrimination in the letting of contracts. It is time the Government committed to regional fairness in government procurement contracts and treats western and eastern Canada as part of the economic family of Canada.

subtopic: CONFERENCE OF FEDERATION OF CANADIAN MUNICIPALITIES
CONFERENCE OF FEDERATION OF CANADIAN MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to be able to attend, along with my colleague from Nepean, a conference held by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities in the beautiful city of Vancouver this past weekend.
One of the issues highlighted at the conference was a deteriorating condition of watermains, sewers, bridges and roads in municipalities across Canada.

I want to congratulate the Federation and its members for their commitment to solving these serious problems.

It is time for the federal Government to resume its traditional role as a partner with the provinces and the municipalities. I encourage Members from all sides of the House to work with us on this national crisis so that we may ensure a sound economy, healthy environment and public health and safety for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the Toronto-Peterborough-Havelock Line Passenger Association for its realistic efforts to preserve the VIA Rail service.
VIA officials have identified this train and the Quebec-Windsor corridor as the two lines that come closest to paying for themselves. The Passenger Association, in a recent presentation to the President of VIA, demonstrated a willingness to work with VIA to rationalize this service.
The Association stated, and I quote that it "strongly supports the Government's desire to minimize VTA's dependence on the public purse," but stressed that VIA must be free of its regulatory stranglehold and allowed to operate as a true business venture. The Association listed a number of eminently practical suggestions for making the train more economical. This is an outstanding public-spirited initiative by these passengers to keep the Toronto-Havelock line open. I hope the proposals receive the detailed consideration they warrant.

Mr. Speaker, the Government's proposed 9 per cent goods and service tax is proving to be an implementation nightmare for the small business person in this country. There are two major problems for small business.
First, there is the problem of compliance. We will now have a two-tier taxation system. The small business will now have provincial and federal taxes to calculate on each item not exempted. Administratively, this will be a quagmire.
The second major problem with the goods and service tax is an economic one. GST is not revenue neutral and
increased prices of goods and services will be passed on to the consumer. It is predicted that the average Canadian family will lose $1,000 per year in purchasing power. This reduction in buying power will result in a drop in consumer demand and thus have a very serious effect on the small business sector.
For a government that has said it recognizes the importance of the small business community in the Canadian economy and have promised to cut down on red tape, they have again shown their disdain for small business. Hiring up to 25,000 new people to collect the tax and complete the forms will only add to the problem. Small business is very concerned that this goods and service tax is just the beginning of further assaults on the economic viability of the small business community in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out once again a deficiency in the Canada Pension Act. As a result of the current test of recency provisions, a number of disabled persons have had their otherwise legitimate applications for Canada Pension disability pension rejected.
There are several hundred disabled Canadians who, when they left their employment, in fact qualified for CPP disability pension but were unaware of its availability to them. When they subsequently learned of the disability pension and applied for it, they were denied because their years of contributions no longer met the test of recency.
These disabled Canadians paid into the Canada Pension Plan. The lateness of their application, lateness owing in some cases to the nature of their disability, ought not to disqualify them from a disability pension. I, therefore, urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty) to seek the appropriate amendments to the legislation in order to accommodate these deserving Canadians.
June 13, 1989

Mr. Speaker, the tenacity and determination of the Canadian Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in dealing with Washington on acid rain have paid off.
Yesterday, the American Administration tabled a bill under which the United States will cut sulphur dioxide emissions, an essential component of acid rain, of which a large part comes to Canada, in half by the year 2000.
When they met in Montebello last week, the governors of the Eastern United States said that pressure from the Canadian Prime Minister had forced the United States to take acid rain seriously and to act quickly.
Our Government has always said that acid rain is a top priority for it, and the initiative proposed yesterday by the United States, after eleven years, is a promising step in the fight against a problem that has destroyed 14,000 Canadian lakes.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, much work remains to be done on this issue, but yesterday's announcement gives Canadians and my colleagues hope that they will finally see their efforts rewarded.

Mr. Speaker, on Sunday last in my riding of Northumberland, I had the moving privilege of witnessing three First World War veterans do the honour of burning the Port Hope Legion's 17-year mortgage. Unknown to us at the time, on that same day the most honoured of Northumberland's First World War veterans, Charles Smith Rutherford, was called to his final rest.
Charles Rutherford brought great honour to the riding of Northumberland. He was the last surviving winner of the coveted Victoria Cross which recognized his heroic service in the First World War. As a member of the Fifth Battalion of the Canadian Mounted Rifles he saw active
service in the trenches of France where he single-handedly captured 45 of the enemy and assisted in the capture of 35 more. This and other acts of gallantry deservedly earned him Britain's top military award as well as two other British medals-the Military Cross and the Military Medal.
Charles Rutherford is quoted as saying his greatest reward for surviving the war was to return to his home at Colbome, Ontario. Though he was humble about his own accomplishments, as Canadians we can all be proud of him and for him and be forever grateful for his service and sacrifices on our behalf.
On behalf of Canadians everywhere, especially those in Northumberland, I wish to extend my sincere sympathy to his children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

Mr. Speaker, in the testimony of expert witnesses before the Environment Committee over the past several weeks the deterioration of the atmosphere has been an overwhelming theme. It is obvious that ordinary citizens throughout the world do not yet fully grasp the stark implications of that subject for the very survival of mankind, unless we are willing and able to manage such critical environmental issues as the ozone layer, global warming and air pollution in all its forms.
Not only will such management be essential in Canada, it will be even more critical on an international and world basis.
The compelling challenge is not just scientific or technological, even more it is political in terms of achieving world-wide consensus and co-operative action.
This week we received a hallmark decision toward such an international accord on atmosphere management with the announcement by President Bush of new clean air policies in the United States which commit themselves to acid rain reductions that significantly affect Canada. This news is not just significant for the merits of acid rain controls which it brings, but even

Oral Questions
more it sets a precedent for two countries working together politically to manage the atmosphere.
There is now a real basis for confidence that a formal acid rain treaty will follow as a political model which will eventually evolve to encompass other atmosphere issues, and will eventually extend to include all nations of the world.
In terms of managing the atmosphere, nothing less will ever be sufficient.

subtopic: DEFACING OF SYNAGOGUE AND SCHOOL IN NORTH YORK
DEFACING OF SYNAGOGUE AND SCHOOL IN NORTH YORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a political philosopher of years gone by observed that the price of freedom is vigilance. That point was brought home last weekend by the cowardly acts of mindless vandals perpetrated on the grounds and building of the Shaarei Shomayim Synagogue and Yeshiva Yessodei Hatorah School in the City of North York.
Ours is a country which has institutionalized the concepts of religious and cultural tolerance. In affording others respect for their uniqueness, and according them the right to lead their lives in dignity, we as Canadians have reaped great material dividends. However, it would appear we have yet to conquer the small-mindedness and the malice of a minority within our midst. Their actions harm the innocent and diminish our worth as a people.
Happily, the real Canada and true Canadians behave differently. My riding association, whose membership includes among others Canadians of diverse origins including Guyanese, Portuguese, Greek, Macedonian, Italian, Scottish and Indian passed a unanimous resolution condemning the vandalism and calling on the authorities to act swiftly and aggressively to eradicate this cancer from our midst.
We must reassure all minorities and the Jewish communities of Eglinton-Lawrence and elsewhere that, when they hurt, we all feel the pain.
I know that this House-the ultimate expression and defender of freedom, equality and brotherhood-will concur.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGES TO U.S. CLEAN AIR ACT
PROPOSED CHANGES TO U.S. CLEAN AIR ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the action of U.S. President George Bush for introducing new measures to protect the quality of the air. The proposed changes to the Clean Air Act will significantly reduce acid rain emissions from the United States.
The plan calls for the reduction of sulphur-dioxide and nitrous oxide emissions that cause acid rain. The reduction requires emissions to be cut in half by the year 2000.
The Government of Canada, in its commitment to the protection of the environment, is committed to cut in half sulphur-dioxide emissions by 1994, and has placed a permanent cap on sulphur-dioxide emissions of 2.3 million tonnes.
I welcome this important announcement since it establishes a united approach in building for our common future.
I look forward to the day when both countries will experience the improved environment that will result from our combined efforts.

subsubtopic: U.S. PROPOSALS TO CUT ACID RAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Prime Minister. Canadians are certainly pleased that we finally have a U.S. President who recognizes that acid rain is a problem that requires congressional solutions. However, congressional solutions are not always international solutions.
We in the Liberal Party are extremely disturbed that the Bush proposal contains no specific monitoring the sulphur-dioxide emissions and, in particular, that there is no over-all cap in the creation of sulphur-dioxide emissions. In other words, if an American power plant is built tomorrow that exceeds the standards, according to the President's proposal, that would be okay.
June 13, 1989

Does the Prime Minister agree with us that the lack of an over-all cap and the specific lack of monitoring provisions are serious omissions? If he does agree, what specific action will he take to lobby for changes in Washington to the Bush proposal?

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: U.S. PROPOSALS TO CUT ACID RAIN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know that my hon. friend and all Members of the House will rejoice with all Canadians in the very substantial step forward taken yesterday regarding acid rain.

subsubtopic: U.S. PROPOSALS TO CUT ACID RAIN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: U.S. PROPOSALS TO CUT ACID RAIN
speechtext:
As expert observers have pointed out, this is the first major initiative by the American administration in 12 years. I think it is good news for Canada and good news for all Members of the House who have been deeply involved in trying to pursue clean air on this side of the border as well.
My hon. friend points out possible omissions from the legislation. I think we should wait to see what the legislation will look like when it is brought before the House of Representatives and the Senate of the United States. We will comment on it then. However, I can assure my hon. friend that we will be as resolute, as patient and as persevering as we have been from the very beginning to bring about the happy result of yesterday.

subtopic: REQUEST AS TO WHETHER THE PRIME MINISTER WILL
REQUEST AS TO WHETHER THE PRIME MINISTER WILL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Bush proposal has serious shortcomings that will continue to kill maple trees, for example, in Quebec. One of the shortcomings is the lack of a ceiling on sulphur dioxide emissions. I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether he has specific proposals to make today in order to improve the legislation that will be presented in Washington and to improve the Bush proposal, because, as it stands now, Canada has no guarantee that the Bush plan will let Quebec's maple trees thrive, and I think that is important.

subtopic: REQUEST AS TO WHETHER THE PRIME MINISTER WILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since my friend referred to Quebec, she would no doubt like me to point out the very enthusiastic comments from Quebec Premier Bourassa, who said yesterday evening that Mr. Bush's initiative was just
Oral Questions
wonderful for Quebec and Canada. So I think that is good news for Quebec and the rest of Canada.
As for possible shortcomings in any legislation, we will follow the situation closely and I can tell the Hon. Member that I have invited Senator George Mitchell, the Senate majority leader, for an official visit to Ottawa next week. The scope of the legislation proposed by the American Administration will definitely be on the agenda then.

Mr. Speaker, in the Bush proposal, the emissions trading proposition or the permit to pollute, has been described by a U.S. Senator as a situation in which a permit to pollute may be given to certain polluting companies in the northeastern United States, something which will do nothing to improve the difficult situation of acid rain which is currently raining on Canada. That is a concern not raised by the Liberal opposition but by a Republican U.S. Senator from Minnesota who has been actively lobbying for changes in the sulphur dioxide emissions regulations in the United States.
Does the Prime Minister have proposals which will ensure that the transboundary problem of acid rain, acid rain from the United States which is raining on Canada, will be specifically monitored in the legislation? Will there be specific provisions to ensure that the permit to pollute which will be permitted under the Bush proposal will not be given to companies in the northeastern United States to the detriment of the acid rain problem in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, the point raised by my hon. friend underlines again the importance of the negotiation by Canada of a bilateral accord with the United States in the area of the control of acid rain. This notion, of course, has been denigrated by certain commentators who suggest that legislation before the American Congress of itself is sufficient. We take the view that there must be that kind of important legislation which the President referred to yesterday and it must be followed by an acid rain bilateral accord which we will negotiate with the United States of America.

June 13, 1989
Oral Questions
With regard to any deficiencies in the legislation as it works its way through the Congress, I have already arranged for Senator George Mitchell, the majority leader of the United States Senate who is from Maine, to come to Canada on an official visit. One of the important considerations between us will be a detailed discussion of the acid rain legislation and the manner in which we hope it will benefit both Canada and the United States.
While there are clearly imperfections in any proposal, I think my hon. friend, with her interest in the environment, will recognize and salute the fact that yesterday was a red letter day, and I underline that phrase, for Canada and for all of us who believe in the environment.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to pose a question to the Prime Minister on this subject. While properly complimenting the President of the United States on his initiative, the Prime Minister has neglected to mention the real delay that we are facing in Canada in replacing the close to $1 billion worth of dirty U.S. coal that is presently used in Ontario Hydro generating plants with sulphur-free coal from western Canada.
Aside from one or two small research projects, no progress has been made in meeting the 1992 deadline that was set. Is the Government prepared to get a guarantee that that importation of U.S. coal with heavy sulphur content will be replaced by western coal by 1992? Is the Government prepared to make major changes to the freight rates as an incentive to bring about that very important development?

Mr. Speaker, because of the initiatives undertaken by the Deputy Prime Minister, there has been an increasingly large percentage of western coal used in the process, if there are continuing serious problems with Ontario Hydro, I know my friend will speak both to me and to the Member right behind him from Willowdale, and we will get this corrected together.

Mr. Speaker, the progress made to date has been one research project worth $800,000.1 am talking about a $1 billion commitment that would bring about the movement of close to 10 million tonnes of coal from western Canada so that Ontario Hydro can meet emission standards in just over two years. That requires a commitment from the Government of Canada to deal with the transportation problem primarily dealing with freight rates which are presently allowed for lumber and grain. It is cheaper to bring coal from Wyoming than it is to bring it from Alberta. Will the federal Government take an initiative to change that situation so we can solve the acid rain problem and help western Canada develop at the same time?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while I appreciate the Hon. Member's interest in this very important issue, I should remind the House that the Hon. Member was a Member of a Government which did absolutely nothing during its term of office to promote the use of western coal.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Furthermore, he was the Transport Minister at that time and he did absolutely nothing.
There has been, through the task force that was put together, a tremendous amount of progress made. I would ask the Hon. Member to check with the Premier's brother who will indicate, I am sure, that the level of western coal that is being consumed by Ontario Hydro in the Province of Ontario has increased substantially. Yes, there are a number of pilot projects which are being funded which I hope will improve and encourage further the use of that coal.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. This Government's financial genius has announced a new sales tax that will put an additional tax burden of $1,000 on the average family, increase the inflation rate by 3 per cent, increase the number of unemployed by 70,000 and,
June 13, 1989

according to a report released today, will also increase the number of tax collectors by between 5,000 and 25,000. Is this true?

Mr. Speaker, I know the Hon. Member likes to ignore things that have been said in the past, but let me just remind him that the NDP tax probe of 1986, when he was the Leader, said, "As well, our analysis had led us to conclude that the current federal sales tax is so unfair, unaccountable and administratively complex that it should be abolished".
Hear, hear.

The fellow who is sitting right behind him said, "Our sales tax system is a total mess". His finance critic in the last Parliament said, "The present sales tax is a bad system and should be abolished. I accept that one alternative is some form of value-added tax such as is being proposed by the Minister of Finance".
Hear, hear!

I cannot be precise about the answer to the Hon. Member's question. The Minister of National Revenue is reviewing this matter. Some of those estimates are wildly out of line, but we are reviewing this matter and some time in the next few months, we will be able to give the Hon. Member a precise answer.
Mr. Speaker, it took the Minister five minutes to deal with irrelevant matters and then he came around to answering the question.
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, the Minister might have added that he also said that any reformed tax should be revenue neutral, and unlike the Minister of Finance, we would stand by our promise. He promised that but he brought in one that was not revenue neutral. We also called for corporate tax reform including a minimum tax which the Minister of Finance also ignored. Don't give us your baloney and answer the question, how many new tax collectors-
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Minister of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party made some observations. I do not know that he put a question, but let me comment on a couple of his observations.
He talked about revenue neutrality. I have made it very clear, and I will make it clearer when the technical paper comes out, that the new tax will replace the existing tax. It will bring in and finance some income tax offsets that will be particularly helpful to people in lower and middle income brackets. After that there will be no additional moneys for the Government of Canada. That will be set out very plainly later on this month.
The second point the Member talked about was corporate tax reform. We did reform the corporate income tax system. It was brought into play last year, and we have seen a significant increase in the amount of corporate tax revenues. In addition, in this Budget we brought in a large corporations tax which I have yet to hear the Hon. Member saying is a good thing. It raises a billion dollars from his friends in the corporate community.
Hear, hear!
Oh, boy, you are going to bring a tear to my eye.
Oh, oh!
There are, Mr. Speaker, some 86,000 companies that made profits last year which don't pay a penny in tax. That is the reality.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance a supplementary question.
We have a genius package of taxes including this new sales tax which the Government is going to bring in. The sales tax is going to increase unemployment by 70,000, inflation by 3 per cent, add $1,000 a year to the tax bill of the average family, and now, according to this report, add some 5,000 to 25,000 tax collector jobs here in Ottawa. Is this the Government's view of justice or economic insanity? Will the Government come to its senses and withdraw this tax now?

June 13, 1989
Oral Questions
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, when the Hon. Member talked about this corporate minimum tax and 86,000 companies that are paying no tax, let me remind him that the large corporation tax applies to all the largest corporations in Canada. There are 3,600 of these. Where are the other 86,000? They are small businesses. They are businesses that are spread all over this country in small communities, communities very heavily involved in the resource sector that are very cyclical.
Baloney.

The Hon. Member says "baloney." If the Hon. Member knew what he was talking about on this, he would not raise this whatever because it is going to destroy employment in all of the small communities right across the country. If we have a corporate minimum tax that is exactly what it will do.
Let me also comment on another point the Hon. Member made. He says that this is going to raise the tax bill by $1,000. Where did he get that information? Is this out of the New Democratic research organization? We have said that families earning less than $30,000 a year will be better off after this tax reform.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Finance. It is about the budget leak.
Not again.

For weeks the Minister has been refusing to answer questions about the security of the budget process, and he has been using the police investigation as an excuse.
This morning the Deputy Commissioner of the RCMP confirmed that, in fact, the security arrangements were not under investigation by the RCMP. The RCMP reported that there were conflicting reports on that subject. The Deputy Minister of Supply and Services says that the security arrangements are now under review.
In light of this, why has the Minister been refusing to answer questions about security except to say falsely, as it turns out, that the leak did not result from negligence, carelessness, or lack of proper security arrangements?

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure what the Hon. Member's question is. We have said on a number of occasions that we review the security procedures on an ongoing basis. Where it is possible to improve these security procedures, we are doing so.
I should say to the Hon. Member that we have under way an extensive review to make sure that things are going to be improved where it is possible to do so, and that will take place in time for the next Budget.

Mr. Speaker, that does not sound like the Minister who said in the House, as reported at page 1005 of Hansard, "that the violation did not result from negligence, carelessness or lack of proper security arrangements", although that may well have been so.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the Minister of Justice.
This morning the RCMP also confirmed that in fact it had sought and received advice from federal Justice officials, federal Justice officials, in deciding whether the public interest would be affected by laying charges against a journalist.
In the light of this honest statement by the RCMP, why has the Minister been giving us only the half-truth that the charges were laid after consulting with law officers of the provincial Government in Toronto?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I made it very clear that the RCMP consulted with the law officers of the Province of Ontario. The law officers of the Province of Ontario asked for discussions with Justice officials.
I note my hon. friend said "in deciding". In my hon. friend's question he used the term "in deciding". It is very clear that it was the RCMP that made the decision to lay the charges after consultations.

After consultations. That is right.
June 13, 1989

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Labour regarding the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety.
Canadian occupational health and safety statistics are alarmingly high. One statistic shows that more than 800,000 work days are lost annually to disabling injuries. Given this astounding figure and given the fact that the Government will cut $1.5 million from the centre's funding this year, why is the Government saying that the centre will close unless it becomes self-financing?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the critic from the Liberal Party, the Hon. Member for Hillsborough, for asking this question. I think it is very important that we state categorically that the centre is not going to close.
It has been very successful since its inception ten years ago in collecting and disseminating worth-while information about safety in the workplace. We are definitely going to see that that the centre will maintain its very worth-while operations.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same Minister. It again concerns the centre. The centre was established in 1978 to "promote the fundamental right of Canadians to be provided with health and safe workplace information", as he said. The Minister himself has said that the centre has "been doing good, useful work and that it should continue."
Is the Minister now saying that the fundamental right of Canadians to this information will be sacrificed for the sake only of deficit reduction?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker,
I would like to point out that since it was established and during the six years the Opposition party was in power, the Centre received $20 million in financial support, an average of $3.3 million per year.
Oral Questions
Since this Government came to power, the Centre has received $40 million over a period of five years, which breaks down to $8 million per year. I think that shows this Government's concern for the health and safety of our workers, and we have simply asked the Centre to continue its cost recovery policy which it started to implement three years ago.
In the course of discussions I had with representatives of the Board of Directors and the Director General of the Centre, it was established that there were many ways in which the Centre could become self-financing within the next few years.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade, and it is related to the Maquiladora program of manufacturing goods in Mexico, trans-shipping them back into the United States, and importing them into Canada under the Free Trade Agreement.
I would like to bring to the attention of the Minister the following notice given to the employees of the Bovie Manufacturing Company of Lindsay, Ontario. I will read a couple of paragraphs which state:
The Mexicans are waiting.
Your strike vote last night means as soon as you go out, the Mexicans will get your jobs immediately.
You may lose 8-10 weeks more wages as you cannot apply for UIC while on strike-
However, if you work until the end of our coverall and lab coat contract, which will be approximately the end of April, and we lay you off, the waiting time is only two weeks.
Remember, if you strike, there will be no job for you to come back to.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: Who wrote that?

The management of this company sent it to its employees as a threat as to where their jobs would go-
Has the Minister taken steps to prevent Canadians companies using the Maquiladora program, an agreement between the United States and Mexico that allows the use of Mexican labour to produce goods without

Oral Questions
tariff coming into the United States and then trans-ship them into Canada as American goods. What is the Minister going to do about it?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was about a year ago when the first false report of the threat from the Maquiladora program was uttered by a Liberal supporter, so the Hon. Member is a year behind the Liberals, and he is 100 years behind the truth.
The situation is the following. Under the Free Trade Agreement there are clear rules of origin so that any goods assembled or produced in Mexico in that manner would not meet the rules of origin and could not be admitted duty-free or whatever to Canada. That is quite clear.
The hon. gentleman should do a little research before he rises in the House and makes such silly statements.

Mr. Speaker, far be it from me to embarrass one of the rare breeds, a Tory from Newfoundland.
The date on this memo is February 23, 1989. The contract referred to is a contract that the goods will still be shipped back into Canada. To fill the existing contract, the goods will still come back into Canada.
It is the Minister who is out of touch. He has only five people in his whole Department to monitor this. The goods are coming back because only five people cannot investigate all those goods. Why does the Minister ask the companies to do the self-complying? Why is the Minister not complying?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been Tories coming into this House from Newfoundland since 1949, while Members of the NDP have been constant shrinking violets. Now they are not even shrinking. They are not even around any more. There are not any of them in the House.
With respect to the supplementary question asked by the hon. gentleman, you had to be a genius to figure out what the question was, by the way, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the Hon. Minister could do his best.
Mr. Speaker, I have to agree that I flunked out on being a genius.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the great majority of Canadians were delighted to hear the news when President Bush announced the proposed acid rain control legislation.
I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs and his officials will have a great deal to do with the process. I wonder what are the implications for him in his position and his officials?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me begin by expressing my appreciation, and I am sure that of other Members in the House, to the Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka for his active interest and leadership.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This has been a long fight for Canada waged particularly vigorously over the last four years.
As the Prime Minister indicated, we will be watching very closely the details of the legislation when it comes in. We will be consulting with Senator Mitchell when he is here next week. We will continue to apply the same determination to ensuring that Canada's environment is protected from this point forward that helped contribute to the announcement by President Bush yesterday.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF NEW SALES TAX ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
As of January 1, 1991 and thanks to his new sales tax, two-thirds of Canadian small businesses will be on the federal sales tax roll.
June 13, 1989

Under the present auditing system, there is one auditor for source deduction, one auditor for sales tax, one auditor for federal income tax, and if we add all the provincial acts and workmen's compensation boards, small businesses spend one-third of their energy responding to audits by various governments.
Could the Minister of Finance give us the assurance, once his new sales tax is introduced, that there will only be one audit at the federal level? I know he doesn't control the provinces, but could he at least give us the assurance that there will be one federal auditor, so that small businesses and businessmen can concentrate on running their operations and producing jobs?

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF NEW SALES TAX ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has identified an area that we have been quite concerned about as far as the proposed sales tax reform has developed.
If the Hon. Member would refer to the top of page 26 of The Goods and Services Tax booklet, he will see identified a number of areas that we are proposing to introduce with the goods and services tax proposal that will reduce the compliance burden for the small business community. These have been discussed at some length with the community itself. We believe that this will go a long way to answering the concerns that have been expressed by them.

Mr. Speaker, if we had to rely on the first phase of tax reform to reduce the paper burden. Small business is concerned about the second phase of tax reform. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business has demonstrated veiy clearly that it is against this tax because it will complicate the lives of those in small business.
Will the Minister of Finance commit himself and his Government today that, with the introduction of the new federal sales tax, we will have one system of auditing so that we can assure Canadians who want to start then-own small business that they will get relief from routine and almost daily inquisition by the Department of National Revenue?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member is not suggesting that we continue with the existing sales tax.
Oral Questions
I am talking about auditing. Do not change the subject.
I think the Hon. Member is agreeing with me-
I am not agreeing with you. You know better than that.

-that we should not stay with the existing sales tax because it is a very complex tax for those companies that are participants in that system.
There are 22,000 separate agreements with the 75,000 taxpayers in the existing federal sales tax system. That indicates how arbitrary, complex, and difficult it is for those businesses to comply.
We believe that the proposals we set out in the document we released six weeks ago, which will be broadened with the technical paper that comes out in a few weeks' time, will show very clearly how much we are concerned about this and to what lengths we have gone to reduce the compliance burden for the small business community.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF GILBERT CLEMENTS

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF GILBERT CLEMENTS
speechtext: I wish to draw to the attention of Hon. Members the presence in our gallery of the Hon. Gilbert Clements, Minister of Finance and Environment, Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF GILBERT CLEMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. The Minister knows that he has broken five of his Government's nine guidelines in promising to grant a Canadian bank licence to American Express. No Canadian bank would get similar treatment in the United States. No foreign applicant has ever been granted this type of special treatment before. Why the special treatment for American Express?

June 13, 1989
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the Hon. Member that in the case of American Express, we are talking about an internationally- known financial institution. Since mid-1986, this institution has been involved in discussions with the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, to consider what it must do to meet our standards. So if American Express, as the Hon. Member said, is not regulated in the United States, its bank will be, in Canada, at the appropriate time. We also indicated, in order to enable Parliament to discuss these regulatory proceedings, that we would postpone the granting of letters patent to American Express until after the new legislation of financial institutions has been introduced and debated in the House.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVERSATIONS WITH AMERICAN EXPRESS OFFICIALS
REQUEST FOR CONVERSATIONS WITH AMERICAN EXPRESS OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also for the Minister of Finance.
The Minister knows that his officials quite properly held up this request for more than 24 months. The Minister himself was so ashamed of this deal that his Order in Council was held up until the final hour, November 21, 1988, election day.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVERSATIONS WITH AMERICAN EXPRESS OFFICIALS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVERSATIONS WITH AMERICAN EXPRESS OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. James Robinson, Chairman of American Express, coincidentally led the pro-free trade lobby in the United States during Canada's last election.
In light of all these unusual circumstances, will the Minister commit to us and to all Canadians that he will make public all conversations that he or the Prime Minister has had with James Robinson or other American Express officials, conversations leading to this unprecedented deal for special friends?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONVERSATIONS WITH AMERICAN EXPRESS OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had no conversations with Mr. James Robinson or any other American Express officials.
The work that was done was done in the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. As my colleague has said, this particular series of discussions goes back to early 1986, I believe it is, well before the Free Trade Agreement. It was a complex set of discussions. It was for that reason that the negotiations took a long period of time.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Fisheries.
Representatives of more than 35,000 fishing industry workers from both coasts are here today to defend their industry and to support the long-standing requirement that Canadian caught fish be processed in Canada. On November 17, 1987, the Minister of Fisheries said:
I give you my assurance those jobs are saved.
Eighteen months later every major fishing industry spokesman states that jobs will be lost. Gutting of the east coast fishery is not far behind.
Will the Minister of Fisheries today repeat his guarantee that no Canadian fish workers will lose their jobs as a result of this Government having put in Canada fish processing regulations on the free trade chopping block?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is unfortunate that the Hon. Member, who is the official fishery spokesman for the New Democratic Party, would raise this kind of alarmist charge in the House of Commons.
It is your statement.
Mr. Speaker, it is passing strange that he has not made such assertions in the many months that he served as critic.
Oh, oh!

In fact, the new landing regulations which were the product of extensive consultation with the west coast fishing industry are designed to enhance and preserve the integrity of our management system for the Pacific salmon and herring industry. These measures are GATT consistent and will be proven to be so. They will preserve the jobs and the long-term integrity of this important resource into the future.
Mr. Speaker, I will not say that the Minister was not here when I raised this issue previously, but I will say that another Minister responded on his behalf.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Minister's own estimates acknowledge that the Department does not have sufficient numbers of inshore and coastal vessels to carry out enforcement on either coast.
Today we learned that the tracker aircraft fleet that patrols the Atlantic fishery is being phased out. How can the Minister of Fisheries expect that his limited landing requirements will work when patrols are inadequate? Without effective surveillance, how can he ensure that there will be no direct sales to Americans on the fishing grounds?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Once again, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member who should know better spreads alarm and exaggeration with respect to the commitment of this Government to provide adequate support scientifically, enforcement-wise, and management-wise for the fisheries of both coasts.
It is for that reason that we have increased the budget of the Department of Fisheries and Oceansin these difficult economic times from $600 million a few years back to well over $750 million, increased enforcement on the Pacific coast from 100 officers in the early 1980s to well over 150 officers, and added helicopters and fixed wing aircraft patrol flights which were never previously operated to manage and enforce our coastal fisheries properly.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. The Minister said in an article in The Ottawa Citizen on June 8 that the federal Government may hike funds for road construction.
Oral Questions
Will the Minister give this House and all of Canada the assurance that he was serious in his statement to the press and that the provinces and the municipalities can now expect federal assistance in road construction?

Mr. Speaker, I am always serious when I make statements to the press or before the House of Commons.
What I said-and I repeat it today-is that we are working at the federal level with the provinces, with the CCMTA which is the group representing the Ministers of Transport of Canada, on a national highway system.
There are three or four different phases. The first was in 1987-88. We are working on another one. Of course we considered, as much at the provincial level as at the federal or national level that something could be done in terms of a highway system. It did not involve at that time, however, putting in more money this year or next year. It was a question of defining the national highway system and working with the provinces to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
Based on that answer, based on the article in The Ottawa Citizen, and coupled with the Ontario Government's announcement in The Brockville Recorder and Times yesterday that a four-lane highway from the nation's capital to Highway 401 would become a reality much earlier than expected, with the early engineering studies starting this year, will the Minister give his assurance that the federal Government will contribute to the funding of this $340 million project which will facilitate traffic flow in and out of the nation's capital?

Mr. Speaker, I am very sympathetic with the Government of Ontario, but I would like to remind my friend that the Government of New Brunswick has put forward a program for $1.6 billion. We have said that it has to be seen within the national perspective.
I cannot give any commitment to the Government of Ontario today other than to say that we all are working together on a national highway policy. We consider that it will be a part of the national transportation policy in the future. However, we could not commit any money and my friend will understand that. Looking at the transportation system in this country, the Government in

Supply
Ottawa is not ready to commit more money to this when we have to deal with our own obligations.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. In my riding there are 25,000 senior citizens. Many of them are suffering because of the Budget. According to the Minister's own Budget documents, if interest rates were lowered by 1 per cent, the deficit would be reduced by $1.6 billion. Senior citizens in Canada earning less than $20,000 are paying $567 million in income tax. If the Minister were to request that the Bank of Canada lower the interest rate by one-third of 1 per cent, it would then give seniors a tax free revenue of $20,000. Does the Minister not think this is a better use of resources?

Mr. Speaker, certainly I think we should look to the Hon. Member for advice on this because I believe he was an adviser to the previous Government when interest rates hit 25 per cent. He is an expert on high interest rates.
The point that he is raising is a serious one. We want to get interest rates down in this country. We made that very clear in the recent Budget. We also said that the Budget itself was designed to give the Governor of the Bank of Canada the scope to reduce interest rates. It is precisely for that reason that we feel we must get the deficit down, so we can get a better balance between interest rate policy and budgetary policy. That is the overriding objective. If we can get the budget deficit down we believe we will see lower interest rates.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt on a single question.

subtopic: CODE OF ETHICS FOR MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
CODE OF ETHICS FOR MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It concerns the question of ethics.
It is reported in today's press that a former aide of the former Toiy M.P. Edouard Desrosiers has sworn an affidavit that other Members of Parliament have stolen federal research funds. That casts a pall on all Members of the House.
I want to ask the Prime Minister how soon we can expect from his Government an ethics package that was promised to Parliament and the people of Canada? As long as this kind of charge is left on the record it is a cloud over all Members of the House.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subtopic: CODE OF ETHICS FOR MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is referring to some very serious allegations which may, in fact, affect all Members of this House. I strongly advise the Hon. Member and all our colleagues that, if they have any knowledge of any actions that may be inappropriate, they have as we all do a duty to transmit all this information to the RCMP so that it can investigate specific cases. I think that is the duty of all the Members of this House.

subsubtopic: COMMENTS BY MEMBER FOR BEAVER RIVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in my office earlier today I caught the exchange between the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader (Mr. Cooper) and the Whip of the Official Opposition. The Opposition Whip and, I must add, the Table, were perfectly correct. My votes in Hansard yesterday are recorded as I intended, yea on the first vote, and I was going to abstain on the amendment and the second vote. I certainly apologize to the Government if my wording confused it.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Duhamel:

That this House call upon the Government to take steps to enhance the federal commitment to the support of post-secondary education, scientific and technological development, job training and re-training and the battle against illiteracy, all of which provide the essential foundation for building a strong and competitive future for Canada.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock, the Hon. Member for Halifax (Ms. Clancy) had the floor.

Madam Speaker, while the financial gain regarding funding for universities has been unfolding, there has been no concomitant re-assessment of our social policy regarding tertiary education. In integrating university education into our policy web, increasingly the Government has begun to equate accessibility to university with universal programs.
The truth is that universities are selective. But they are selective on the basis of aptitude and ability, not on the false premises of wealth, position, sex or cultural background. Every Canadian does not want to go to university. Not every Canadian can or should graduate from a university. Universities are charged particularly with the creative process of education and must be the trustees of change. People still fail to accomplish what universities expect of them, and that is as it should be. That is why we have developed alternative forms of post-secondary education.
In creating the rhetoric of accessibility and social rights with reference to university education, however, we have lost this perspective and come seriously close to undermining the capacity of the institutions to deliver the calibre of education which is fundamental to our future. A part of this argument deals with institutional autonomy which in some minds is in conflict with accountability. Some people are dedicated to proving that the two are not mutually exclusive and that autonomy does not imply licence. Rather, institutional autonomy reflects the need for a university to be free to foster creativity in every sector of endeavour.
It also means that universities must be free to maintain a critical mass of knowledge transfer. In other words, even if society thinks that the only need is for engineers, the university knows that a knowledge of history, of languages and of literature is fundamental to progress in any civilization. This is expensive. One of the best
Supply
epithets I know comes from Derek Bok who said: "If you think education is expensive, try ignorance".
The other truth is that this kind of change cannot be manipulated or managed in the policy sense. You just have to ensure that the context for creativity exists. The creation of that context is not cheap, but it is not something which Canadians have ever balked at paying.
When I started university in 1966, we imported much of our professorate from the United States and we got the Grade B teachers who were not good enough for the Ivy League but fine for the colonies. This theme, unfortunately, has resurfaced and we now hear about the fact that we will not have enough home grown PHDs to staff our universities in the next generation. These cannot be created overnight unless we devalue the principles of credential, although there are a lot of creative possibilities for evolving our educational system so that it is more responsive to social needs and more fully integrated from one level to another.
There is a crucial need for a new national debate on education. The forum on post-secondary education held last year was intended to do this, but it fell far short of the goal. It did gather a lot of obvious representatives but it did not generate the kind of coverage needed by any of the participants and has not resulted in the kind of discussions that would lead to a re-assessment of where tertiary education fits in our social priority, let alone what it is.
Such a debate must be encouraged. It must be rigorous and critical. The rhetoric of the 1960s must be replaced by a fuller understanding of what the options and requirements are, including funding and a government commitment to supply that funding. We have to know the timeframes and the adaptations that universities are making to contemporary demands. As difficult as it is, we must come to some collective understanding of what we want the educated Canadian of the future to be. We need a strong co-operative plan of action and we need it now. We cannot afford budget cuts that threaten our educational and thus our cultural future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as usual, I have listened with great interest to the comments of my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Halifax (Ms. Clancy). Whereas in the past she has been correct, there is no sense to this nonsense, in this case she has made very good sense on a number points, particularly as she has rightly said that
