there is much that must be done in this country in what I know as post-secondary education. Tertiary is another word over five letters and I am lost. Is it the same thing?
Yes. Third level.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Thank you. The question we all face is having an education system that suits and meets the needs of a country that must grow technologically and must meet the demands of the future, with a workforce and population that has the capability of not only to deal with those challenges but increase our capability.
There has been some discussion of the Saskatoon conference which in itself was a landmark event in this country. While the Hon. Member points out that she would like to see perhaps more come from Saskatoon, or more come from another conference that would have followed on from Saskatoon, it is only fair to point out that there were a number of provinces in this country that objected to Saskatoon even happening.
It is a fundamental of our system that the provinces control education and not a situation which I particularly would want to change. The needs of the individual provinces vary greatly. The history, the culture and the educational demands are such that the provinces should maintain that control.
Recognizing that this is a very fundamental point to a number of provincial governments-perhaps not the Hon. Member's own but governments of some provinces-and recognizing that Saskatoon was a great step, I wonder if she advocates the use of the financial power, for instance, such as we use under the National Health Act, to bring provinces along or to bring provinces in line? If not, how does she reconcile the concern of Liberal governments across this country that the federal Government not meddle in any form of education, primary, secondary, tertiary or post-secondary? I would hate to find the Hon. Member buried in one of her own sepulchres.

Madam Speaker, my hon. friend from St. John's East (Mr. Reid) made several very good points to which I would like to respond.
First, if he had been listening, he would have heard me say that the time has come for change which can only take place through sensitive negotiation between both levels of government as to the path which post-secondary or tertiary, whichever term you prefer, education will take.
My hon. friend also made note of the question of technology in the field of education. I would like to comment on that as well. I noted myself in my earlier comments that technology is the chic area for people looking at the post-secondary-I will use that term as opposed to tertiary today in deference to my hon. friend's sensitivities-but I remind him of the title of an old poem called, "Bread and Roses", and the fact that along with the bread of technology we need the roses of language, literature and other cultural and political pursuits. I would suggest that he not forget those.
I would also suggest to my hon. friend, as he comes from the same hard-pressed region as I do, that we have many universities in our Atlantic region. All of our universities are suffering. Yes, possibly too many. Certainly in my own riding, which has six universities and one on the outskirts, all of those universities play a unique role. There is indeed a place for each one of them. Every single one of them is suffering. They are suffering with physical plants that are falling apart. They are suffering with the highest tuition rates in the country. They are suffering with the lowest salaries for their faculty. They are suffering on research grants. They are suffering on equipment, et cetera. None of this is news to my hon. friend.
What I am saying to my hon. friend is that the time has come, if we are to have post-secondary education, education generally as a national priority, then we have to sit down and make a plan and see where we are going. It cannot be done by the provinces alone.
The Hon. Member's province cannot afford to fund post-secondary education, neither can my province, Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick. For the rest of the country, I am not sure. They have to look at their problems. I have looked at the ones in our region. Those are the realities which we face and we understand them.
To merely say that education is a provincial responsibility and not a federal responsibility and therefore put blinders on and no longer even look at the situation is to
June 13, 1989

abdicate our responsibility. I know that this is not what my hon. friend had in mind. It certainly is not what the Members on this side had in mind.
After eight years of teaching in a university, I have seen what the problems are, as many of my hon. friends on the other side have seen them as well. What we need is a sensible plan, one that which is sensitive to the problems-constitutional, physical, salary, et cetera- that assault our universities on a daily basis. This is not a partisan issue. This is an issue for the future of our country. It is one which needs action instantly.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for York North.

Madam Speaker, the world is in constant change: Glasnost, Solidarity's election win in Poland, AIDS, reproductive technology, the recent student riots in China for democracy. At home we have free trade, our aging population and a post-secondary education system in serious trouble. Important developments in our nation, indeed our world, will experience many changes in the 1990s as we get ready to face the challenges of the twenty-first century.
It is ironic, therefore, that today in the House of Commons and the Parliament of Canada we are debating an issue which is so fundamental to meeting the future needs of this country that one would think that a government would have had the vision to address it before it became an issue on an opposition day in Parliament.
Clearly, the question we must ask is: What is our Government doing to prepare Canada to meet these future challenges? The answer, sadly, is: Not as much as it can and not nearly as much as it must.
Today, I speak to the motion which condemns the Government for its destructive and inadequate policies affecting post-secondary education, research and development, training, re-training, illiteracy and its failure to provide the necessary funding to these areas which are vital to Canada's future.
It is obvious from listening to the Speech from the Throne and the Budget that the current Government simply lacks the commitment and ability to summon a vision for Canada to carry toward the twenty-first century.
Supply
Indeed, the Government's vision of Canada at no time looks more than four years ahead to the next election. The Government's vision is a vision for Canada based on an electoral map.
The people of Canada are dealing with change. They want, need and expect government to lead the way. Education should be treated as a vital national and international priority. The relative economic strength of nations has always been determined by their ability to educate and train their people. That is truer today than it has ever been in the past.
Education is vital to Canada's future. However, you could never tell that by looking at federal Government policies and programs. Indeed, Canada's per capita investment in post-secondary education is less than it was five years ago.
Federal cuts in shared cost programs with the provinces have reduced funding to post-secondary education equal to the total budgets of the University of Toronto, the University of British Columbia, the University of Alberta, McGill and Dalhousie. When quality education is more important than ever, the federal Government has chosen to cut back. The Government must begin to wake up to the reality of this nation and this world. Today we live in a technological age. Our economy is information-based and we do business in a global market-place.
Canada's youth today must have a future and must be able to deal with the challenges of the global village. Regardless of their chosen field of study and career orientation, our youth must be well educated and have a thorough understanding of the math, science and technology and, at the same time, a knowledge and awareness of the humanities and social sciences. As the countries and markets draw closer and closer together, communication among people becomes more and more important. Our young people must be able to communicate so that our message does not get lost.
When we consider the unbelievably fast pace that this world is moving in, the increasing flow of information, goods and services, financial transactions among nations, continuous flow of discussion, debate, compromise, agreements between nations, it is only logical that the nation which better trains, educates and provides opportunity for higher learning will undoubtedly have an economic, social, cultural and political advantage. Investing in our universities is absolutely crucial to meeting

June 13, 1989
Supply
the demands of the global village, the village whose reality must be addressed in a serious way.
When we think of post-secondary education, we must realize that it is the way to open doors for future generations. We cannot build a strong, prosperous society in financial, social and cultural terms if we as a people are not able to understand the world around us. Post-secondary education gives our people the opportunity to become more and more masters of our own destiny. As a country, we must realize that knowledge is power and it is extremely necessary in maintaining self-determination as a nation in global affairs. An educated people is the answer to the challenges facing us today and in the future.
My concern is that we are not doing things we have to do to ensure Canada's ability to master the challenges it faces. The Government's answer to this reality that I expressed earlier is the following: Despite the obvious economic and social benefits associated with a highly educated population, Canada's universities are currently experiencing severe financial problems.
In 1986, the Government passed Bill C-96 which reduced the growth rate of transfers to the provinces by 2 per cent over five years, 1986-1987 to 1990-1991. The Government would have saved approximately $5.7 billion. The portion of financing for post-secondary education that was to be cut amounted to $1.6 billion. As if that were not enough, the Tory Government, beginning in 1990-1991, will further reduce the growth rate of the Established Programs Financing transfers to the provinces by 1 per cent.
Given the free trade deal environment and the need to be able to compete with our neighbour across the border-indeed everyone in the global market-place- we must for all the more reason be sure that we have a well educated workforce and a competitive economy. All this occurs at a time when enrolment and the need for post-secondary education is at its peak.
In the near future in Canada, almost half the new jobs will require more than five years of combined education and training above and beyond high school. Reduced funding for post-secondary education will seriously threaten its quality and accessibility. Without increased government support for post-secondary education and the development of strategy for post-secondary education and training, our youth will not be able to face the challenges of the years to come. Rather than compete in
the world, we will slowly fall farther and farther behind our competitors, such as the United States, West Germany and Japan.
Disorganization and lack of leadership has marked the Tory Government's attempt to deal with the deficit crisis. What has happened now is that our youth have to pay for it. The deficit, in budgetary terms, is obvious to all. Now what has become also apparent is a deficit of solutions. Future accessibility to our universities is in jeopardy.
I would like to conclude my remarks by requesting that the Government fulfil immediately its promises to provide sufficient increased support for post-secondary education, research and development, training and retraining programs which constitute the cornerstones of a strong, competitive Canadian society. I want to give back to young Canadians the dreams of our forefathers, the dreams and goals that brought people to this country and made us a great nation: The dreams of freedom, dignity, fulfilment and perhaps the greatest dream of all, the dream of equality and accessibility. Equality and equal opportunity to learn, equal opportunity to work and equal opportunity to succeed.
Thus, I call on the Government and my colleagues to recognize the importance of this issue. We cannot go from here where we want to go and where we want to be unless we begin to put programs in place and into effect and realize the importance of post-secondary education.
We are a resource rich country here in Canada, but the greatest resource of all is our people, especially our youth. It is now time to make education the number one priority. We cannot afford to block the major artery to Canada's future.

Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for York North (Mr. Bevilacqua) for taking part in the debate and I would like to remind him that it is not only a question of money, because he stressed the reduction in transfer payments. As far as my department is concerned, the Department of Science and Technology, I think that we have done a lot. His colleague just said that we had to change. I think that the change has begun, because the Minister of Science and Technology and all the other ministers of science and technology throughout the country have signed a policy to train all young people across the land, so that in all provinces, young people will have an equal opportunity, all Canadians will have the same chance to
June 13, 1989

enter useful occupations that can improve the quality of life for Canadians.
I would like to point out to my hon. colleague that this national policy that the ministers of science and technology adopted involves asking industry to cooperate much more in training young people to meet the needs of industry.
We have noticed, Madam Speaker, that students naturally go into the social sciences and humanities; they go more for medicine than for science. On the other hand, we have noticed that what sometimes gives other countries an advantage over ours is that many more people go into scientific disciplines, Madam Speaker.
I would therefore like to ask the Hon. Member for York North what evidence he has to support his statements that we are not interested in university research, when the facts speak for themselves.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think the Hon. Member meant to ask a question of the Hon. Member for York North.

Madam Speaker, what really concerns me about the question and the comments made by the Hon. Member is that they are focusing into a particular area. However, I think that my speech was all encompassing as far as a philosophy and as far as a method and a vision for education as it relates to building our country.
The Hon. Member stated that in other countries there is a certain focus given to an education policy. I think that the most important thing is that students should also have the liberty to choose exactly what they want to do. To the point raised by the Hon. Member, if that is indeed the direction that this Government would like to take, then why have we not seen, for example, the development or any talk of a national apprenticeship program on that side of the House? As you know, in the past election, the Liberal Party of Canada went right across the country stating that we indeed require a national
Supply
apprenticeship program. So I think that we are in agreement.
We can speak of certain issues and what we have done in positive ways, but the reality is that this Government has developed a tunnel vision approach when it comes to the deficit. In reality, what it is really concerned about is the deficit of solutions and deficit of ideas to address the problem of the deficit. The reality, as I said earlier, is the fact that transfer payments to the provinces have been decreased once again. As I have mentioned, to the tune of almost $1.6 billion for education. So you cannot as a Government begin to take credit for a very small portion of the program on the one hand while on the other hand leaving some people out in the cold and not allowing them accessibility to a post-secondary education. We as a people and as a Government have a moral obligation toward students and young people. I think that post-secondary education should be looked at as a right, not a privilege. It is a right of citizenship. That is the way in which we as a country should be directing our resources in terms of our vision of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on the Government's commitment to support post-secondary education and literacy. It is my first opportunity in this session to address the House. It gives me an opportunity to reflect quietly on November 21 and the visions set out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that day, his concerns for continuing to build a caring society, the vision for the future and the pathway to the 21st century. It also gives me the opportunity to say how pleased I am to be the Member of Parliament for Pierrefonds-Dollard, encompassing the cities of Ste-Genevieve, ile-Bizard, Dollard-des-Ormeaux, Pierre-fonds and Roxboro the so-called North Shore area of the West Island. Also, I would like to say how pleased I am to be able to work on behalf of and with the Government in areas of restoring and giving greater equality and social justice.
Yes, there was restraint. Yes, we did share the burden. Yes, we did believe that we could not continue to pass on the debts to future generations and that we had to do something about them now. However, we have a considerable program available-and some $450 million for

June 13, 1989
Supply
these programs of equality and social justice in the areas of official languages, women's programs, minority and cultural communities and natives. In fact, we will be having more program funding for the disadvantaged and the doubly disadvantaged. Certainly, we are touching on one of those areas today. Thus I am very pleased to have this opportunity to be before the House today.
Our record is a solid one in both the areas that we are discussing today, our commitment to post-secondary education and literacy. As I will show, we have maintained and enhanced our support to all aspects of higher education and literacy because we understand the importance of Canada's human resources, both to our social and to our economic development.
Our basic commitment was set out in the Throne Speech of October, 1986. It is one from which we have not deviated.
We said then that the Government was committed to supporting with the provinces and the territories a system of post-secondary education based on excellence and equality of opportunity. These twin themes of excellence and equality of opportunity run through the initiatives we have taken to support higher education for the past few years. As well, they are the basis for our continued commitment to co-operation with the provincial Governments and for the funding we provide through federal-provincial transfers.
I might just quickly note that I kept hearing from the Hon. Member for York North (Mr. Bevilacqua) about decreases. I do not know how more money can ever be a decrease. To me, more money is always an increase. We are maintaining our commitment to support post-secondary education. Our transfers for PSE and health will increase by $1 billion from 1989-90 to 1990-91. Over the next five years the EPF will provide $25 billion more than over the past five years. That is an increase in any language.
I would now like to give an overview of the federal role in providing financial support to post-secondary education. This has evolved over time and now encompasses four main expenditure areas. They are contributions to the provinces and territories for general assistance to post-secondary education, usually called Established
Programs Financing or EPF; support for research, some by federal Departments, but the bulk via the three research granting councils, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Medical Research Council and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council; student financial assistance, primarily by means of the Canada Student Loans Program but also through awards provided by a variety of federal Departments and agencies; and other direct federal responsibilities such as the higher education of Armed Forces personnel, of inmates in federal correctional institutions and of Canadian Indians and Inuit.
For 1989-90 it is estimated that the total amount of federal government support in these four areas will be in the neighbourhood of $7 billion. When one considers that Canada now spends over $12 billion annually on post-secondary education, the significance of the federal government support becomes readily apparent.
About 75 per cent of the $7 billion is provided to the provinces and territories by means of tax and cash transfers under the EPF. There was some element of doubt expressed by Members opposite as to where we stood in terms of the world, with respect to how we were competing aggressively and competitively with the world about us and in terms of how we were maximizing the use of our human resources. From what I have been advised, we are second in the world in terms of PSE participation, close behind the United States. We are one of the three highest countries in terms of education spending, very close to Sweden and The Netherlands.
We must, of course, be concerned that we stay in the forefront of developed nations. That is why we are stressing post-secondary education based on excellence and equality of opportunity. Our program of Canada scholarships and centres of excellence, plus our support for granting councils are important contributions to excellence in science, research and higher education.
On the subject of EPF, I would like to stress that the federal transfers to the provinces for post-secondary education and health are not only very large, but are still growing substantially. Following the recent Budget, it is estimated that EPF transfers will continue to grow at a rate of nearly 5 per cent annually.
June 13, 1989

To be more specific, it is estimated that the total value of the EPF transfers for health and post-secondary education will be $19.8 billion in 1989-90 and $20.9 billion in 1990-91. EPF will provide $25 billion more to the provinces over the next five years than over the last five years.
Of these totals the federal legislation identifies some 29 per cent as being in respect of post-secondary education. Translated into dollars, this means that the post-secondary share of EPF is expected to be about $5.7 billion in 1989-90 and $6 billion in 1990-91, up from $4.2 billion in 1984-85.

In other words, federal contributions to post-secondary education are extremely generous and increasing steadily. In the same area, other major federal support programs were spared during the latest budget cutbacks, and I am referring to the Canada Student Loans Program, the Official Languages in Education Program and also the Canada Scholarship Program and the centres of excellence.
At this point, perhaps I may offer more detailed information that will give a clear picture of our commitment to supporting post-secondary education. In this respect, the latest updated information may be found in the 1987-88 Report on Federal and Provincial Support to Post-Secondary Education, tabled in the House on April 7 this year.
In addition to established programs financing, the federal Government provides financial support to the provinces and the territories so that they can pay the additional cost involved in maintaining and developing official language minority education programs and second official language teaching at all levels: primary, secondary and post-secondary.
Bilateral agreements, representing a total of $199 million in 1987-88, provide the framework for contributions made under the Official Languages in Education Program. These contributions total $57.2 million at the post-secondary level.
In addition to these contributions, the federal Government provides direct assistance to the provinces and territories. A total of $18.1 million has been granted for
Supply
other activities such as the Summer Language Bursary Program and the Monitor Program.

With respect to student assistance, under the Canada Student Loan Act, the federal Government provides loan guarantees to post-secondary students with demonstrated need. The main feature of the Canada Student Loans Program is the fact that the federal Government pays the interest on these loans while the students continue full-time studies and for six months afterward. In 1987-1988, the total value of new loans was $589 million. The cost of interest on outstanding loans plus program expenses was $211 million in 1987-1988. In addition, the federal Government paid $77 million as an alternative payment to Quebec as that province has always opted out of the program since its inception in 1964.
I would be remiss if I did not mention that a wide variety of federal Departments and agencies also provide scholarships, bursaries, fellowships and other support to post-secondary education students for a total of $143.4 million. The federal Government also provided close to $600 million in 1987-88 for university research, about $500 million of which went to the three research granting councils. The remaining sums came from the federal Departments and agencies that provided grants and contributions related to their own areas of responsibility by contracting out research required for their own internal purposes and by providing other research-related services.
Finally, in respect of its constitutional responsibilities for education, the federal Government spent a total of $104.1 million for its three military colleges, its Canadian Coast Guard college and for post-secondary education courses for federal inmates. As well, the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs spent $73.6 million in support of native post-secondary education in 1987-1988.
To summarize, the federal Government makes transfers to the provinces and territories under the EPF arrangements and the official languages and education protocols. It provides direct support to post-secondary students either through loan guarantees or awards such as scholarships and bursaries. Mainly through the work of the research granting councils, it provides support to university research and it assumes its own constitutional responsibilities for education.

June 13, 1989
Supply

The federal Government plays a very active role in this respect because it sees itself as a partner in supporting post-secondary education, and as such, it pursues the following objectives: to encourage institutions to offer programs and services that are in line with broad national objectives such as official languages, multicul-turalism and promoting the status of women; to provide financial assistance to the provinces through the established programs financing system, enabling them to provide accessible and high quality post-secondary education; to provide financial assistance for research and development; and finally, to fulfil its own constitutional obligations with respect to the education of Native peoples, armed forces personnel and other specific groups.
In line with these broad national objectives, the Government, as I said earlier, maintains its focus on excellence and equality of opportunity.
I am sure Hon. Members will understand that, for the sake of Canada's future, we must do everything we can to help our colleges and universities aim for excellence in education. The future of our country is at stake, if we want to keep up with an increasingly competitive world.
Making post-secondary education accessible should also remain one of our major concerns. We already have one of the most open and most accessible systems in the world, and we must maintain our emphasis on equality of opportunity.

Let me outline some of the achievements of the Government in the field of post-secondary education over the past two years. We held the first national forum on post-secondary education, an historic collaboration of federal and provincial Governments with universities, colleges, the private sector and other interests. We organized, under the sponsorship of the Prime Minister the first national conference on technology and innovation, much of which was focused on the contribution of higher education and university research to Canada's competitiveness.
The Canada Scholarships Program has been introduced to encourage 2,500 of our brightest young men and women to enter science or engineering each year. The Centres of Excellence program will provide $240 million to support projects that will enhance our ability
to compete internationally. Doubling the number of CIDA sponsored students and trainees will benefit both our own higher education system and the countries which receive our aid. Our support for a French language college in Ontario and le college de l'Acadie in Nova Scotia will improve opportunities for francophones outside Quebec to study in their own language at the post-secondary level.
These examples show that the Government is already fully committed to supporting post-secondary education for Canada's future. Let me now turn to the Government's commitment to tackling the problem of illiteracy.
Illiteracy is a national problem. In every town and village, every region and district, every city and metropolitan area in Canada, there are men and women who cannot function in everyday life because they cannot read and write. Two years ago, Southam News commissioned a survey which revealed for the first time the full extent of illiteracy in Canada. I remember being shocked by the survey's findings. I know every Member of this House was equally shocked, equally dismayed and equally determined to end illiteracy.

Illiteracy is expensive! According to a study by a business task force, it causes annual losses of around $4 billion in the private sector and $10 billion in Canadian society as a whole.
However, the cost is highest at the personnal level: there are men and women who cannot read the newspaper or make sense of the bus timetable; they cannot take a full and active part in community life.

The road to literacy is one shared by all of us. The road to literacy is not followed exclusively by one level of Government. It is not followed by one political Party. It is not followed by the private sector alone. It is a road of partnership, of shared effort and of shared energy.
On September 8, 1988 we announced that the federal Government would be one partner among many in the journey on the road to literacy and we are working with many partners. Two weeks ago, the Government of the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador said in its Speech from the Throne that it was committing greater provincial resources to literacy. Advisory councils and task forces have been set up in Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia to work with the provincial Governments on literacy. Ontario, New
June 13, 1989

Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and the two territories have all increased spending on literacy programs.
Quebec has passed legislation guaranteeing all adults the right to complete their secondary education. There is no limit on age or level of financing. This measure, which is unique in Canada, will help to increase literacy in the province.

I notice you signalling, Madam Speaker. I am deeply appreciative of having had an opportunity to work in these particular areas. The issue of literacy is an important one for all of us. We have now developed a very important partnership with the provinces, with those dedicated people who have worked in the field for countless years, very often strangers in the wind, looking for an oasis in the desert. We have been more supportive of those groups. We have found new partnerships to build on. We are now bringing forward initiatives with the business and labour movements and with the voluntary sector. Having 25 per cent of Canadians functionally illiterate is shocking, intolerable and it is something we must work to eradicate.
We will continue to do everything we can through the programs in my Ministry, programs that will be working to provide greater equality and social justice. We will do all that we can to make sure that this becomes a more open, more accessible, more understanding society and that we continue to be a country of freedom and opportunity which will continue to give all of the members of our community a full opportunity to participate. It is then and only then, Madam Speaker, that we can really take our place and say that ours is the great country of the 21st century able to challenge other countries of the world in the knowledge that we are much more effective and productive when we use the full capacity and full potential of all Canadians.

speechtext: Questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Prince George- Bulkley Valley.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister for his comments. I have a brief comment to make and a question to put to the Minister.
The Minister will know that I forwarded to him earlier in the year a report that had been prepared by residents of the Prince George, B.C. area who are arguing for a university in that community. I will be making some comments on that later in the afternoon. I appreciated the information which the Minister provided to me.
My question relates to the transfer payments to the provinces. There have been allegations, perhaps across the country but certainly in British Columbia, that the provincial Government has perhaps used those funds since they have not been, as has been put, tagged to be spent on education and health care. In fact, in British Columbia from the Social Credit Government the charges are that health and education money has been used for pavement on highways.
Has his Department done any studies to establish whether those charges are, in fact, correct? If his Department has, would the Minister be prepared to make them available to the House?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad my hon. colleague recognizes that significant funds are transferred and, indeed, we are hopeful that they are being fully used. We realize that there is a lot of goodwill involved here. We work in close collaboration with CMEC, the Council of Ministers of Education, Canada. We have a very good relationship with all of the Ministers of Education. We meet from time to time. There is a genuine feeling on the part of us all who serve at any level of Government to continue to make sure that our young people are the most competitive in the world, the best trained and the funds being advanced in this particular area are used for the purposes that they are intended.
The Member is certainly in the knowledge that this is somewhat of a complicated nation, that there are jurisdictional differences and it takes, as a great Quebecer, Frank Scott, once said: "When you deal with issues of this type it takes realism and goodwill. It takes co-operation, not confrontation." We will continue to work

June 13, 1989
Supply
actively with our provincial colleagues for the delivery of service, which is their jurisdictional area, but certainly as I indicated in my comments this afternoon, we have a vital interest. We want to make sure that Canadians and young Canadians are completely qualified and competent and can challenge anybody in the world today.

Madam Speaker, I did not hear the answer coming through as forcefully as I would have liked it.
On several occasions all across the country, university professors as well as student federations have called upon the federal Government to introduce some sort of a mechanism whereby whenever they are putting money toward education and passing it on to the provinces that that money be used for education. Unfortunately, that has not happened as of yet.
I want to just quote from an article published by The Ottawa Citizen today, contrary to what the Minister was saying "that we are fairly well equipped internationally to compete", which quotes a statement of Lynn Burton who is a senior adviser to the Prime Minister's National Advisory Board on Science and Technology.
To be quite blunt, Canada is ill-prepared for the new world
competition and for the changing environment.
She goes on to state:
-that figures from the 22-country Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development show that Canada lags in several key areas, including employee productivity, vocational training, quality of skilled workers and worker motivation.
That is true. We have been saying these things for years. When the Hon. Member was on the opposite side of the House he made those statements. We are both saying today that illiteracy is one of the major causes of lack of international competitiveness when it comes to Canadian society.
Unless we make education a national priority, unless we make illiteracy a national issue and we deal with those who think on that basis, we will be spinning our wheels in the air. It is very important that the Minister start addressing this issue with a little more seriousness than just telling us about the federal commitment to educational illiteracy. I know the funds are there. I know the Minister made a statement over the past two years to put some money toward illiteracy. He has set up an agency. He is doing very well and I have to commend him on that.
Since we have all of this confusion would the Minister be prepared to set up a national strategy to deal with education, namely, a National Education Act whereby you can set standards? We can set the bible for the provinces to follow. We can set the ABCs on how we want to see our kids prepared for the future.
In my view, no way can we carry on in the international market the way we are now with over 70 per cent geared toward the service sector rather than the manufacturing sector.
I would appreciate if the Minister would respond.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I certainly appreciate my hon. colleague's recognition of the great progress we have made in fighting illiteracy. It was this Government that last September brought a $110 million program forward. I recognize that the Member might say "What's $110 million in an over-all field of $50 billion?", but that is very significant. We not only set up a small secretariat of veiy, very dedicated officers who are working well on the initiative, but we brought forward initiatives with the provinces and the territories. I was able to sign agreements with nine provinces and two territories by the end of March of the last fiscal year. Prince Edward Island, I believe, is the only one that we missed out on. We were not quite ready with them. We have agreements with Quebec, Ontario and all of the other provinces building new partnerships. In each one of those cases new funds were advanced for new projects and new community commitments to help eradicate illiteracy.
We went further. We are now building partnerships with the business people, with labour organizations, with new participants, individuals who were not involved in the so-called literacy movement before but we have not forgotten the dedicated volunteers who worked for decades on the issue, often without any helping hand.
As far as The Ottawa Citizen is concerned, while I have not seen the article personally, I would want whoever wrote it to be able to reflect also on the information that I have been given as advice that we are one of the three top countries in terms of educational spending. We rank with Sweden and The Netherlands. We are second in the world in terms of post-secondary education, very close behind the United States. We do not have to be ashamed of anything that our young people are doing. We are the equal of anyone in the world today. In fact, when we make full use of all our citizens by letting us all be completely involved, which is what I work for in another

area of my endeavour, on the multicultural and citizenship side, watch how much more productive, competitive and effective we will be.
On a recent trip I had the opportunity to visit a company operated by two individuals who had come into this country in the early 1950s from Germany without two nickels to rub together. They are now running a business which employs 800 people who have come from 50 different cultural communities. That company is doing $50 million to $70 million worth of business, and looking forward to doing $150 million worth of business in the future. That is the type of competitiveness that we are developing.
What am I doing? We work very actively with the provincial Ministers in the Council of Ministers of Education, Canada Committee. We have initiatives and aims in common. There is no confrontation. This is co-operation. All of us recognize the need and the ability to deliver better by working together. The national forum was a focus that brought forward important initiatives. I will be meeting with my colleagues, the provincial Ministers, in the very near future and certainly will continue to look for ways to build a stronger and better system together.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased today to have this opportunity to speak on this motion that in many respects deals with our responsibility as leaders in Canada to the youth of this country and to the students of this country. There is a distinction there, Madam Speaker, as more and more of today's students, although they may claim youthfulness, as you and I do ourselves, are much less youthful than students of previous generations.
The decisions made now will provide for the foundations of a strong Canadian economy, a country that will be equipped and able to compete globally, whose people have the necessary educational background and technical skills, as well as the intellectual skills that will enable us to compete in the changing global economy.
This is a particularly timely motion. As universities and colleges were in the process of winding down their regular academic terms, it was announced in the federal Budget that transfer payments to the provinces for
Supply
health and post-secondary education would once again be capped.
At the same time, the Government is creating the new Department of Industry, Science and Technology which is intended to have the purpose of stimulating and being responsible for science, research and development in Canada
Finally, the Government has introduced Bill C-16 to create the Canadian Space Agency. At the same time, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), in openly contemptuous remarks, criticizes the very people who will be the foundation of that new agency for expressing hesitation about moving their families from the areas where they live to the south shore of Montreal.
Previously, I have spoken in the House on the Government's rhetoric in the area of science and technology. It has a lot of rhetoric, and I believe it is mostly good. Unfortunately, the substance has not been particularly grasped, nor has it been shown to have action to follow it. After all, it was the Prime Minister of Canada who, in the September, 1987 edition of the University Teacher's Bulletin wrote: "This Government stands ready to co-operate fully with the provinces and all others involved in post-secondary education and will help create and maintain a system of higher education capable of meeting the challenges facing Canada."
In the light of that statement by the Prime Minister, Madam Speaker, I invite you to accompany me on a brief journey across Canada to some of the post-secondary educational institutions on which we rely.
First, let us visit Memorial University in Newfoundland, the first and largest university in that province. At first glance one cannot help but notice how well it is used, or perhaps overused. Memorial University was built to accommodate 7,000 students. It now attempts to educate 12,000 students.
In Nova Scotia, one is struck by the fact that tuition costs are the highest in the country. That is a reflection of the fact that over the last 12 years tuition has doubled in this country. In British Columbia, tuition has tripled.
In Ontario, at the University of Toronto, join me in a fight to get a seat in Psychology 100. For the information of Members, the lecture is held in Convocation Hall. At the University of Windsor, the library selection has so badly deteriorated that students have been referred by

June 13, 1989
Supply
their professors to Wynne University or the University of Michigan to do their research and reading.
At Carleton University in Ottawa, from which I am proud to have graduated, biologists are using outdated equipment in their labs, making measurements unreliable and morale very low.
In British Columbia, it is not uncommon for students to arrive in September to register for classes only to find there is no room for them. What is as crazy as the campus of Kwantlen College in Surrey, British Columbia? It is a campus composed entirely of portables. I am told the only thing that is permanent on the campus is the sign.
At the University of Regina, buckets are dispersed throughout the buildings to catch the rain. This is only a reflection of the larger problem of underfunding in that institution. It is clear that we have compromised our educational system.
In 1864, Theodore Rand, the Superintendent of Education for Nova Scotia stated words which are still appropriate today: "Is not education in fact the power of the people to make all the resources of their countiy tributaiy to their interests and comforts? And is not this the most obvious and prominent distinguishing feature between an educated and an uneducated people-the power of the former, and the powerlessness of the latter, to develop the resources of nature and providence, and make them subservient to human interests and enjoyments?"
There is no question of the importance of science, engineering and technology to Canada as we move into this globally competitive market-place. There is also no question of the problems we face. In the past in the House we have talked of the ratio of research and development expenditures to Gross Domestic Product. The Prime Minister promised to increase it to 2.5 per cent from where it currently resides at around 1.4 per cent. The GERD ratio, as it is called, is a misleading indicator. It may indicate that we do have a problem, but there are other things that are more significant.
There is a lack of industrial research in Canada. There is a flagging commitment to government research and to basic fundamental research. There is a massive trade
deficit in high technology and medium technology goods. To me, those factors are perhaps more important than the ratio of research and development expenditures themselves, much as we would like to increase that.
Post-secondaiy education and Canadian universities are key to Canada's competitiveness and ability to do fundamental research. There are very serious problems in addition to the ones that my example suggested. There is the research capability. The number of research scientists and engineers in our universities is largely determined by the teaching requirements of the institutions. Those have remained pretty static since the early 1970s with the consequence that our university engineers and scientists are now middle-aged. They are not yet at retirement age. We have gone through a period of years when people holding PhDs have had difficulty finding positions in Canada. As this group of scientists and engineers reach retirement, we will have difficulty replacing them. Therefore, we are going from the problem of having a shortage of jobs for our PhD holders to the reverse problem of an inadequate number of PhD doctors to fill the university positions.
There is underfunding for basic research. I wish to refer the House to the report of the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology formed by the Prime Minister. In its university committee report it states on page 43:
Because of inadequate funding, individuals and groups at the forefront of their disciplines in Canadian universities cannot undertake venturesome and leading-edge research projects. Success is likely to be achieved late in the process, only after leading foreign research universities have established their pre-eminence in new scientific trajectories.
Few large groups of scientists thrive in Canadian universities. When a notable innovation is achieved, the advantage tends to be lost shortly after to better-funded groups abroad who are in a position to exploit the opportunities it can provide.
We lack a policy in Canada on what might be called big science, major projects. When do we fund them and with what resources? What resources are directed from other scientific endeavours? We face the problem of obsolescence in our laboratory facilities in the universities. The estimates of the need to raise the level of our scientific and technological equipment to a satisfactory level have been massive. The National Sciences and Engineering Research Council estimated $50 million per year is

required. In fact, we have been spending $10 million to $15 million per year.
The problems are massive. We need certainly the renegotiation of the EPF arrangements. We need to increase the budgets of the granting councils. We need to increase research funds available to the environmental sciences. In conclusion, Madam Speaker, we need to integrate our endeavours in science, research and development with those of the industrial sector as well as our concerns about maintaining a clean and healthy environment.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, I listened closely to the speech by the Hon. Member for Ottawa South; he said that the universities' equipment was completely outdated and that this problem occurred all over the country.
I think that the Government is aware of this problem. That is why, in its Inovaction program, the Canadian science and technology strategy, the Government, together with the provinces, set up a task force to deal with this problem and other related matters. It will certainly have solutions to suggest to us.
It is important for us too that universities have facilities with the latest technology. We think it is absolutely essential for the students and the researchers who must follow the students' progress very closely.
I would like to say to the Hon. Member that the centres of excellence program is one way. The $240 million that the Government has allocated for centres of excellence is a way for the universities and researchers to get the very sophisticated equipment that they need. But of course, they must apply for it and you know very well, Madam Speaker, that a committee is now dealing with the selection of the centres of excellence.
Supply
But I want to say to Hon. Members that this is an approach for researchers and I think that those people are very aware of it and they have been very enthusiastic in making proposals to the Government.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member, because I heard him criticize and say that the Government was not giving enough money to this and that; I would like the Hon. Member to tell me whether he and the members of his party would be in favour of increasing the deficit to give the money that is being requested all over the place. That is the question I have for my hon. colleague.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the Parliamentary Secretary for her question.
First, I agree that the centres of excellence program is a good one. It was developed by Mr. Peterson's government in Ontario and it is now being applied by the federal Government. I believe that this program has a lot of merit.
Concerning the deficit-

With regard to the deficit, this is a very important issue. I know that nobody on this side would trivialize the importance of the deficit. As it was said earlier this morning, if you think education is expensive, you ought to check out the price of ignorance. There are some things in Canada that should be regarded not as expenses but as investments. It is absolutely essential to the future well-being of Canada that we adequately fund our educational institutions. There can be no other choice. We talk about the problem of the deficit putting the expenditures of today onto future generations. What a burden we put onto future generations if we burden them with ignorance. Therefore, although I think the deficit is an important issue, I think that the deficit that exists in our intellectual development, in our scientific and technological endeavours and engineering vis-a-vis the rest of the industrialized world is much more serious to Canadians and to our future than is the financial deficit.

Madam Speaker, my question will be short and I want to put it to my hon. friend from Ottawa South. It has to do with his remarks earlier about facing the possibility of a shortage of scientists and engineers somewhere down the road. I am simply wondering whether it is a matter of throwing money at the problem. I know that our hon. friends across the way would

June 13, 1989
Supply
suggest at times that we are not sensitive to the deficit or to the Budget and that we would like to just spend money like drunken sailors. I do not think that is the case. But I want to ask my friend from Ottawa South, is it a matter of just throwing money at the problem? Will it go away by throwing money at it or is the problem much more complex than that?

Madam Speaker, I just have a short answer!

No, we cannot solve the problem by simply throwing money at it. It is a complex problem, but money is part of the solution. If we are going to attract more students into the natural and engineering sciences, we need to ensure that we have job opportunities for them at the conclusion of their educational careers. It was not much of an incentive to undertake a very arduous program such as science or engineering with the prospect at the end of not finding work and having to go off to the United States.
As for the problem that will likely arise in the 1990s of an inadequate supply of Ph.D scientists and engineers in Canada, I think we need to address also the problem of the funding of our facilities ensuring that we have adequate lab and research facilities in our institutions available to encourage students to pursue those disciplines.

Madam Speaker, this Liberal Party motion which is before the House asks the Conservative Government to provide more support to post-secondary education, more support to scientific and technological development in Canada and more support for job training, retraining and the battle against illiteracy. I want to congratulate my colleague from St. Boniface who prepared and put this motion to the House of Commons today for the issues involved in this motion are among the most critical that face Canada in the 1980s and the 1990s.
If Canada is to survive, let alone progress as a major player in world commerce, then education and training must be among our highest priorities. Much more must be spent if we are going to compete in this very competitive world.
We have just signed or implemented the Free Trade Agreement with the United States. We in this Party opposed that agreement, but it is in place now. It has been passed by Parliament. But unless we do more to prepare our workforce, both young and older, to be more productive and more competitive, then we are going to lose. The Americans will gain most of the benefits to be derived from that agreement. Our nation will also be facing competition in Europe in 1992 when the Common Market countries remove nearly all barriers between them. It will be more difficult for Canada to compete in the European market. Consequently, it becomes absolutely essential that Canadian workers be the best trained in the world.
Education is not simply an option or a luxury, it is absolutely essential for our economic well-being. That is why I could never understand why governments at any level could cut back on education and training when we were in a recession or faced with difficult times, such as now when the Government alleges that there is a problem with the deficit. The way to dig out of a recession and to reduce the deficit is to make sure that the workforce is highly skilled and can produce the income and revenues necessary to turn the situation around.
If we look at European countries like West Germany and Sweden, we can see that at times of recession and depression they spend more money on education and training than they do otherwise. They use that opportunity when people are off work due to cyclical or structural changes in the economy to upgrade their training and re-educate them so that they are put in line to take up the new jobs that will come after the recession or depression.
Education and training is like the basic infrastructure for the economy. Just as businesses need roads, railroads, ports and airports, they also need a skilled workforce. Rather than skimp on money in providing for a skilled workforce, it is necessary to put more money into it.
It is also important to do something about the wasted human resources. We have very high unemployment rates in Canada with respect to our disabled population and our minorities. Almost 30 per cent of Canadians are illiterate and there are many drop-outs. These are wasted human resources unless we have appropriate

training programs and education programs to make these people productive, as they all can be.
Switzerland is a small country which does not have very much in the way of natural resources. It does not have a lot of minerals, oil or gas, as Canada has. It does not have large areas for agriculture and fisheries. Yet that is a very progressive country because it has a veiy highly skilled labour force. It is highly skilled in chemicals, machinery, banking and finance. Tourism is another important part of its economy. Every Swiss citizen is skilled to play a role in the economy so that there is very little wasted resource. It is a highly productive economy with only about 1 per cent or 2 per cent unemployment. Switzerland makes the best use of its labour market force, which makes that economy very successful.
As our Party's critic for unemployment, I will deal more specifically with the training and retraining aspects of this motion. I want to refer the House to a recent report that I believe is the best report on the subject before us today. It was published in the spring of 1989 by the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre. The feature article in that spring issue is a review of education and training in Canada. I urge all Hon. Members to read this article because it is short and to the point.
The report states that for the year 1988-89, spending at all levels for education in Canada was about $40.8 billion. It goes on to point out that on a per student basis, Canadian public spending on secondary and post-secondary education represents a smaller proportion of Gross Domestic Product per capita than the average for 17 OECD countries. It also points out that during the 1980s, spending per student in real terms rose at the primary and secondary level in Canada but spending fell significantly at both the college and university levels. It goes on to say that Canadian post-secondary institutions have not been able to make up for reduced government funding and shrinking tuition income.
That is the case with respect to post-secondary education. There has been a drop in funding on a per capita student basis, which is adversely affecting post-secondary education in Canada.
Supply
Let us deal with training. The Conservative Government has cut training and employment programs by 32 per cent since 1984. The budget for training and employment in 1984 was $2.2 billion. That has been reduced to $1.5 billion in 1989, a cut of 32 per cent.
According to a table in this report, in 1982-83 under the former Liberal Government, there were 235,000 Canadians in government-sponsored institutional training courses. After the election of the Conservatives in 1984, this dropped significantly. In 1984-85 there were 216,000; in 1985-86 there were 201,000; and in 1987-88 there were 133,000. There was a drop from 235,000 in 1982-83 to 133,000 in 1987-88, which corresponds to the cuts in moneys available, to which I have already referred.
For example, let us consider what happened with air traffic controllers. This situation has hurt the country significantly in several main centres. In its 1985 Budget, the Government cut moneys for the recruitment and training of air traffic controllers. It only took about three or four years before there were shortages in Toronto, Montreal, Moncton and elsewhere, to the extent that there were no new air traffic controllers available. The Government had to go to the United States to get air traffic controllers and it is now trying to train them here. Another example of cuts in post-secondary education is the Government's recent cut to Indian post-secondary education. We have already debated that in the House. That spirit shown by the Government, to cut in areas of education, is extremely worrying and bothersome to many Canadians.
There is much to be said on this subject but I will conclude by referring again to the report of the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre. This report does not represent the Liberal Party criticizing the Government, or the Opposition in Parliament criticizing the Government, it is the report of a very respected centre set up by labour and management to deal with these issues. They state in their conclusion that the evidence cited in the report suggests that Canadians have not given education and training the priority they deserve. They state that real spending per student on post-secondary education is declining and there is only a limited amount' of job related training and retraining done by both government and employers. That is the issue we are debating in the House today. We will be

Supply
asking Members of the House to support this motion which says that more must be done. I think Canadians will be watching Members of Parliament on both sides of the House to see where they stand on this critical question before the country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I just want to be sure that I heard the Member correctly. I think what he meant to say was that there was an increase in the amount of spending which the Government was having on post-secondary education. Now, there are not any cuts, there is an increase in the amount of money that is being transferred to the provinces on health and post-secondary education, $19.8 billion in 1989-90 and in 1990-91, $20.8 billion. Of these amounts, some 29 per cent is identified as being for post-secondary education. I would hope that the Member would realize that this is a growth of over $1 billion from 1990-91 in the first year of the Budget that we have the restraint program in place. Indeed, there has been an increase in our commitment to fund post-secondary education. The funding will provide $25 billion more to the provinces over the next five years, than over the last five years with $83 billion, for 1984-85 to 1988-89, and $108 billion for 1989-90 to 1993-94. When I hear the Member speaking, it concerns me because the support from the federal Government for post-secondary education has exceeded the support increase from the provinces.
When the Hon. Member said that more money should be spent, I want to ask this Member of Parliament where he would get the additional money to fund these programs which he is speaking of?

Madam Speaker, it seems that the Hon. Member was not listening closely to me. Of course there is an increase in the Budget of this year compared to last year with respect to post-secondary education by this Government. We have not said that there was not.
What we are saying is in the Budget the Government has cut back the rate of increase which was supposed to be there. In other words, the provinces were expecting to get so much but because of this Budget, they are going to get less than they were expecting and on which they were
planning. That is the point. Sure, the Government is increasing it but it is not increasing it by the amount which was committed in the earlier years of this Government.
In the Budget, it definitely cut back on the rate of increase of funds to the provinces for health and education. That is the point.
To deal with the last question of the Hon. Member, we would certainly find more money for education out of the other budgets of the Government. It is absolutely essential that we have a highly skilled and a highly trained workforce.
By the way, this is not Liberal Members who are speaking. I challenge the Hon. Member to read the feature article, Spring 1989, of the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre. This is a centre made up of business and labour. It is not just a labour centre. What do they say? They say that on a per student basis, Canadian public spending on secondary and post-secondary education represents a smaller proportion of GDP per capita than the average for 17 OECD countries. This report is critical of the Government, not just this Government but provincial governments as well for then-commitment to education.
With respect to training-and training is pretty clear- the Government cut 32 per cent from 1984 to 1989. This was a serious cut-back. The figures are there. What has the Government done? It is trying to make it up now by taking $800 million out of the unemployment insurance fund, because it was criticized by the de Grandpre Commission and other commissions for not putting enough money into training and it is going to try and put that money back in. Instead of taking it out of general tax revenue, it is taking it away from unemployed workers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure today to respond to the motion. In fact, it seems to me that the Hon. Member has provided me with an opportunity to make some positive remarks about the accomplishments of our Government.
Our Government does not need to be called upon to take steps to build a foundation for the future prosperity
June 13, 1989

of this country. We have taken those steps. We are well on our way to ensuring a strong and competitive Canada.
During the last four and a half years, this Government has rewritten the book on employment training. We have worked with business, labour, communities and anyone else concerned, to create programs which will best serve Canada, the Canada of tomorrow.
Several billions of dollars have been spent to train and re-train our country's workers so that they can fill the jobs of the future.
In the Hon. Member's riding, this Government has spent $2 million for job training in the last year, and a total of $14.4 million since 1985. He of all people has no basis upon which to base doubts about the efforts to help Canada meet the labour market demands.
Can any Member of this House deny the massive challenges Canada faces in light of expanding global markets and technological change? In a world of enhanced international competition, Canada's most important need will be a workforce which is equipped with proper skills. Our human resources are the key to preparing Canada for a labour market which is radically different from the one we know today.
Right now 40 per cent of all jobs call for professional white collar skills. By the year 2000, 80 per cent of all jobs will demand those skills. It is clear that job training is a critical part of the march toward the next century. Equipping workers for the needs of the labour market will ensure Canadians the degree of prosperity which we have enjoyed until now.
Two-thirds of Canadians who participated in a recent poll said they need skills training to keep up with economic competition and technological change. Less than half who work full time have received training in the last two years. More than half of the unskilled workers polled had received no training at all.
The example of other countries has proven that business must constantly help their workers upgrade their skills in order to keep their businesses competitive. In 1987 only one out of four Canadian companies spent money to train their employees. Canada spends about half the amount on training that the United States does.
Supply
It has been evident for some time now that this is not just the Government's problem.
When Canada cannot keep up with the world competition because its workforce does not have the right skills, it is the problem of every Canadian. That is why our Government since its first term has worked to put relevant training programs on everyone's agenda. Labour, that is business and communities, have an important role to play in providing training.
In 1985, this Government replaced more than 40 ineffective make-work programs with a co-ordinated regionally driven initiative called the Canadian Jobs Strategy. Rather than making work, we set out to make permanent jobs. The Canadian Canadian Jobs Strategy is aimed at individuals and their specific training needs. It allows people in the regions and those who understand the local labour market to direct the programs. Canadian Jobs Strategy has been just as successful as we expected.
Most of those who take part in the Canadian Jobs Strategy training program find work using their newly acquired skills, skills which will continue to be in demand for a long time. Building on the philosophy and the success of the Canadian Jobs Strategy, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) recently introduced an important national program which will lead to further improvements in the training and employment structure of the Canadian labour market. The Canadian Labour Force Development Strategy represents this Government's commitment to work with its partners in business and labour, to prepare Canada's workers for the future. It also represents a shift from former passive income support for the unemployed to more relevant and active support in line with labour market needs.
On examining our unemployment insurance program, we found it needed a new look to keep it in line with the times. The purpose of the unemployment insurance program remains what it was upon its inception almost 50 years ago: to protect people out of work and to maintain economic stability. However, unemployment insurance must evolve with current economic needs. Under the strategy, unemployment insurance will help clients get relevant training so that they can return to the workforce with the skills needed to keep a job longer.
